a41.t:
TEHRAN | TASS | The US Air Force has conducted a successful attack on three Iranian nuclear facilities, and all aircraft have returned to airbases, US President Donald Trump reported on Truth Social.
“We have completed our very successful attack on the three nuclear sites in Iran, including Fordow, Natanz, and Esfahan. All planes are now outside of Iran’s space,” the US leader wrote. “All planes are safely on their way home,” he added.
According to Reuters, the attack involved B-2 strategic bombers previously redeployed to Guam, a US overseas territory in the Pacific. These aircraft are capable of carrying GBU-57 bunker-buster bombs, which are specifically designed to penetrate heavily fortified underground targets.
Experts believed earlier that this type of munition could be used in the strike on Iran’s Fordow nuclear facility, which lies buried approximately 90 meters below the surface.
TASS has compiled key information about the US strikes on Iran.
Attack
– Trump announced the operation via Truth Social.
– The strikes targeted three nuclear facilities: Fordow, Natanz, and Esfahan.
– A “full payload of bombs” was dropped on the Fordow site.
– According to Reuters, the strikes were carried out by B-2 strategic bombers equipped with GBU-57 bunker-buster bombs.
– This marks the first US military strike on Iran since 1979.
– ABC News reported that Israel received advance warning of the operation.
No impact yet
– Experts interviewed by NBC News say the strike on Fordow is unlikely to trigger a nuclear explosion or large-scale radiation release.
– International observers believe the site contained no nuclear warheads or reactors.
– Iranian officials stated that the Fordow facility had been evacuated ahead of time and suffered no irreversible damage.
‘Time for peace’
– Following the strikes, Trump declared that the “time for peace” has come
– He called it a “historic moment for the United States of America, Israel, and the world” and urged Iran to “agree to end this war.”
– CNN reported that Trump does not currently plan additional strikes and is awaiting a response from Tehran regarding negotiations.
– Earlier, Trump had not ruled out a strike on Iran, particularly on the Fordow site. The White House had indicated a decision would come within two weeks.
Abandoning diplomacy
– Prior to the strikes, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio assured European allies that Washington remained committed to a diplomatic resolution, The Wall Street Journal reported.
– Rubio held talks with officials from the UK, Italy, Cyprus, France, and Sweden over a two-day period.
– Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met with European representatives in Geneva, but the negotiations failed to yield progress.
Israel
– For the first time since the conflict began on June 13, no rocket alerts were issued in Israel for over 24 hours.
– In response to the US strikes, the Israeli military tightened civilian restrictions, banning public gatherings and halting non-essential business operations.
Day 10 of escalation
– Israel initiated its military operation on June 13, citing the destruction of Iran’s nuclear and missile programs as its objective.
– Iran responded with retaliatory strikes, including with ballistic missiles and drones.
– Russia condemned Israel’s actions and signaled its willingness to mediate.
– On June 19, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova warned the US against military involvement, cautioning that such interference could lead to “truly unpredictable negative consequences.”.

a114.t:
National Bank of Malawi (NBM) plc has reaffirmed its dedication to maintaining the highest standards in tax compliance following its recent recognition by the Malawi Revenue Authority (MRA).
During the MRA’s 25th anniversary celebrations held at the Bingu International Conference Centre in Lilongwe on Friday, the Bank received a prestigious Certificate of Recognition for its outstanding commitment to tax compliance and invaluable contribution to national development, an honour that, according to NBM plc Chief Finance Officer Daniel Jere, carries deep significance beyond the moment.
“We are honoured to receive this recognition from MRA. It is a testament to our commitment to fulfilling our tax obligations diligently and on time,” he added. “It is a reminder that responsible corporate citizenship is not just about profitability, but about active participation in building our nation.”
Jere stressed that tax compliance is one of the bank’s core principles, and the recognition from MRA serves as a motivating force to uphold and even surpass the current standards. He noted that NBM plc has consistently posted strong financial results, translating into significant tax contributions that support Malawi’s development agenda.
“It is a testament to our commitment to fulfilling our tax obligations diligently and on time. By paying our taxes, we directly contribute to the development of Malawi, and we will continue to uphold this standard as part of our corporate responsibility.
    “NBM plc pledges to maintain the highest standards in tax compliance, continuing to contribute meaningfully to Malawi’s economic growth through timely and accurate payment of taxes,” said Jere.
The Certificate of Recognition comes at a time when the government is intensifying efforts to boost domestic revenue and reduce dependence on foreign aid. By recognising compliant institutions like NBM plc, MRA seeks to promote a culture of accountability, responsibility, and partnership in national development.
The MRA’s 25th anniversary event celebrated the authority’s journey since its establishment in 2000 and acknowledged key stakeholders who have played a vital role in advancing Malawi’s fiscal agenda.

a147.t:
Muktasari:
- Mkuu wa Mkoa wa Kigoma, Balozi Simon Sirro amesema afya ya wananchi ndiyo kipaumbele cha kwanza, hivyo wametakiwa kufuata maelekezo ya wataalamu kuhusu matumizi ya maji ya Mto Malagarasi.
Dar/Kigoma. Serikali mkoani Kigoma imesema wananchi wanaendelea kupata huduma ya maji kwa matumizi ya nyumbani kutoka vyanzo vingine salama, huku uchunguzi wa kitaalamu ukiendelea kufanywa kuhusu vifo vya samaki na viumbe wengine vilivyogunduliwa ndani ya Mto Malagarasi.
Wananchi ambao wamekuwa wakipata maji kwa matumizi mbalimbali kutokana na chanzo hicho, wameacha kuyatumia kutokana na tahadhari iliyotolewa na serikali kwa kushirikiana na wataalamu ili kupisha uchunguzi wa nini chanzo cha vifo vya viumbe hivyo ili kuepuka madhara kwa binadamu.
Akizungumza na Mwananchi kwa simu leo Jumamosi Septemba 27, 2025, Mkuu wa Mkoa wa Kigoma, Balozi Simon Sirro, amesema wananchi wanaendelea kutumia maji kutoka vyanzo vingine salama.
Amesema serikali inafuatilia kuona kama kuna haja ya kuongeza huduma za ziada ya upatikanaji wa majisafi na salama kwa jamii hiyo.
“Maji ya Mto Malagarasi hauwezi kuyatumia, vivyo hivyo kama yalivyo hata bila ya tatizo lililojitokeza. Hata hivyo, kwa sasa wananchi wa maeneo hayo wanapata maji kutoka vyanzo vingine kwa kuwa vipo katika eneo hilo tofauti na Mto Malagarasi,” amesema.
Balozi Sirro amesema serikali inafuatilia kwa karibu kubaini na kuchukua hatua za haraka kama kuna uhitaji kwa lengo la kuhakikisha wananchi hawakosi huduma muhimu za maji wakati uchunguzi wa sababu za tukio hilo ukiendelea.
Tayari kamati maalumu ya uchunguzi imeundwa ikijumuisha wataalamu mbalimbali na imeshaanza kazi kwa kuchukua sampuli za viumbe waliokufa ili kubaini chanzo cha tatizo na kama kuna madhara ya kibinadamu ili kutatua tatizo hilo.
Hali ilivyokuwa
Wiki hii wakazi wa Kijiji cha Kigadye, wilayani Kasulu, walishuhudia idadi kubwa ya samaki wakiwa wamekufa na kuelea juu ya maji ya Mto Malagarasi, hali iliyozua taharuki na hofu kwa jamii inayotegemea mto huo kwa chakula na maji.
Baadhi ya wananchi walisema hawajawahi kushuhudia tukio la aina hiyo kwa miongo kadhaa, huku wakiendelea kunufaika na fursa mbalimbali za mto huo, zikiwamo upatikanaji wa maji kwa matumizi kadhaa yakiwamo ya kilimo, majumbani na vitoweo.
Baada ya tukio hilo, serikali ilitoa tamko ikiwataka wananchi kuacha kuvua samaki au kutumia maji ya Mto Malagarasi hadi uchunguzi utakapokamilika.
Hatua hiyo ililenga kulinda afya za wananchi na kuzuia madhara yoyote ya kiafya endapo chanzo cha vifo vya samaki kingekuwa ni sumu au uchafuzi wa maji.
Ofisa Usafi na Mazingira Mkoa wa Kigoma, Nesphory Sugu alisema kwa kushirikiana na wataalamu wa afya, sampuli ya maji katika mto huo ilichukuliwa kwa ajili ya uchunguzi.
Mganga Mkuu wa mkoa wa huo, Dk Damas Kayere, alisema hakuna mtu aliyepata madhara kutokana na tukio hilo, bali ametoa wito kwa wananchi wa eneo hilo kufika kwenye vituo vya afya iwapo watapata athari zozote kutokana na kutumia maji au kula samaki wa mto huo.
“Afya ya wananchi wetu ndiyo kipaumbele cha kwanza. Hivyo, tunawataka wananchi wote wa maeneo yanayopitiwa na mto huu kufuata maelekezo yanayotolewa na wataalamu,” amesema Balozi Sirro alipotembelea eneo hilo kuona kilichotokea.
Umuhimu wa Mto Malagarasi
Mto Malagarasi ni mrefu na wa pili kwa ukubwa nchini Tanzania baada ya Mto Rufiji. Una mchango mkubwa kiikolojia na kiuchumi si tu kwa Kigoma, bali pia kwa Taifa, ukitoa maji kwa vijiji vingi vya Kigoma na Tabora na kuchangia katika Bonde la Ziwa Tanganyika. Pia, ni makazi ya samaki aina mbalimbali ambao wamekuwa tegemeo la lishe na kipato cha wakazi wa Kigoma.
Kwa sababu hiyo, tukio la samaki kufa kwa wingi limekuwa na athari kubwa si tu kwa mazingira, bali pia kwa uchumi mdogo wa kaya.
Kwa sasa kinachosubiriwa ni kamati ya uchunguzi ambayo matokeo yake yatatoa mwanga juu ya chanzo cha tatizo hilo na hatua sahihi za kuchukua ili kuendelea kunufaika na fursa za mto huo.
a147.en:
Summary:
- The Regional Commissioner of Kigoma, Ambassador Simon Sirro, has said that the health of citizens is the first priority, and they have therefore been asked to follow the instructions of experts regarding the use of water from the Malagarasi River.

Dar/Kigoma. The government in Kigoma Region has said that citizens continue to receive water for domestic use from other safe sources, while a technical investigation continues into the deaths of fish and other creatures discovered in the Malagarasi River.

Residents who had been getting water for various uses from that source have stopped using it following the warning issued by the government in cooperation with experts, in order to allow an investigation into the cause of the deaths of those creatures and to avoid harm to humans.

Speaking to Mwananchi by telephone today, Saturday 27 September 2025, the Regional Commissioner of Kigoma, Ambassador Simon Sirro, said citizens continue to use water from other safe sources.

He said the government is monitoring the situation to see whether there is a need to add extra services for the supply of clean and safe water to that community.

"You cannot use the water of the Malagarasi River, just as it is even without the problem that has arisen. However, for now the residents of those areas are getting water from other sources because these exist in that area, unlike the Malagarasi River," he said.

Ambassador Sirro said the government is following the matter closely in order to identify and take swift action if there is a need, with the aim of ensuring that citizens do not lack essential water services while the investigation into the causes of the incident continues.

A special investigation committee has already been formed, comprising various experts, and it has begun work by taking samples of the dead creatures in order to determine the cause of the problem and whether there is any harm to humans, so as to resolve the problem.

How it happened
This week residents of Kigadye Village, in Kasulu District, witnessed a large number of fish dead and floating on the water of the Malagarasi River, a situation that caused panic and fear in the community that depends on the river for food and water.

Some citizens said they had never witnessed such an event for several decades, while they continued to benefit from various opportunities offered by the river, including the availability of water for several uses including agriculture, household use and relish (food).

After the incident, the government issued a statement asking citizens to stop fishing or using the water of the Malagarasi River until the investigation is completed.

That step was aimed at protecting the health of citizens and preventing any health harm should the cause of the fish deaths turn out to be poison or water pollution.

The Kigoma Regional Sanitation and Environment Officer, Nesphory Sugu, said that in cooperation with health experts, a sample of the water in that river was taken for investigation.

The Regional Medical Officer, Dr Damas Kayere, said no one had suffered harm from the incident, but he appealed to residents of that area to go to health centres if they experience any effects from using the water or eating fish from that river.

"The health of our citizens is the first priority. Therefore, we ask all citizens of the areas through which this river passes to follow the instructions given by the experts," said Ambassador Sirro when he visited the area to see what had happened.

The importance of the Malagarasi River
The Malagarasi River is long and is the second largest in Tanzania after the Rufiji River. It makes a major ecological and economic contribution not only to Kigoma but also to the Nation, providing water to many villages of Kigoma and Tabora and contributing to the Lake Tanganyika Basin. It is also home to various species of fish that have been a mainstay of nutrition and income for the residents of Kigoma.

For that reason, the incident of mass fish deaths has had a major impact not only on the environment but also on the small household economy.

What is now awaited is the investigation committee, whose results will shed light on the cause of the problem and the correct steps to take in order to continue benefiting from the opportunities of the river.

a172.t:
Après son sacre aux Awards de la santé : Fatou Sylla honorée par le Ccm-Côte d’Ivoire
Un concours, rappelle-t-on, organisé par le Réseau des professionnels des médias, des arts et des sports engagés dans la lutte contre le sida et la promotion de santé en Côte d’Ivoire, (Repmasci).
En effet, Fatou Sylla a raflé le 1er prix presse écrite des Awards de la santé pour avoir proposé deux de ses productions portant sur les thématiques liées au Vih pédiatrique et une interview qu’elle a réalisée avec la présidente du Ccm-CI. D’où cette initiative de recevoir la lauréate dans les locaux de la représentation locale du Fonds mondial.
Ce fut donc une belle petite cérémonie conviviale qui s’est déroulée en présence de la gestionnaire de portefeuille de la Côte d’Ivoire au Fonds mondial, Paula Hacopian, de la Coordinatrice pays pour le Plan d’urgence présidentiel de lutte contre le Vih-Sida du gouvernement américain (Pepfar) en Côte d’Ivoire, Ngalamulume Bibola, de ses collaborateurs...
En recevant la journaliste du service société du quotidien Fraternité Matin qui a plusieurs distinctions à son actif, dans les locaux de son institution à la Riviera-Golf, Dr Danielle Adjafi a tenu à féliciter la lauréate mais surtout l’encourager à continuer sur cette lancée.
« Félicitations pour la qualité du travail qui vous a valu ce prix. Nous sommes fiers de savoir que l’une de vos productions qui a été primée concerne les activités du Ccm-CI et surtout du Pnoev. Bonne continuation », a-t-elle dit en saluant le mérite de la lauréate.
Comme elle, Paula Hacopian et la responsable du Pepfar ont exhorté Fatou Sylla à toujours traiter des sujets d’intérêt public, notamment ceux en rapport avec le Vih, surtout le Vih pédiatrique, qui est "une problématique en Côte d’Ivoire". « Vous avez nos encouragements. Nous espérons pour vous des lauriers encore meilleurs que celui-ci », ont-elles félicité la journaliste.
L’édition 2024 des Awards de la santé couplée du 21e anniversaire du Repmasci a eu lieu le 13 juin à la Maison de la presse, au Plateau.
Les productions qui ont retenu l’attention du jury sont intitulées "Dans le quotidien difficile des orphelins du Sida", réalisée avec l’aide du Dr Flore Kouassi Lago, Directrice-coordonatrice du Pn-Oev et une interview de la présidente du Ccm-CI, portant sur les fonds alloués aux personnes atteintes de cette pathologie.
a172.en:
After her triumph at the Health Awards: Fatou Sylla honoured by the CCM-Côte d'Ivoire

It is recalled that the competition is organised by the Network of Media, Arts and Sports Professionals Engaged in the Fight Against AIDS and the Promotion of Health in Côte d'Ivoire (Repmasci).

Indeed, Fatou Sylla carried off the first prize for the print press at the Health Awards for having submitted two of her pieces on themes linked to paediatric HIV and an interview she conducted with the president of the CCM-CI. Hence this initiative to receive the prize-winner at the premises of the local representation of the Global Fund.

It was therefore a fine, convivial little ceremony that took place in the presence of the Côte d'Ivoire portfolio manager at the Global Fund, Paula Hacopian, of the Country Coordinator for the United States government's President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) in Côte d'Ivoire, Ngalamulume Bibola, and of their colleagues...

While receiving the journalist from the society desk of the daily Fraternité Matin, who has several distinctions to her credit, at the premises of her institution in Riviera-Golf, Dr Danielle Adjafi was keen to congratulate the prize-winner but above all to encourage her to continue in this vein.

"Congratulations on the quality of the work that earned you this award. We are proud to know that one of your prize-winning productions concerns the activities of the CCM-CI and especially of the PNOEV. Keep up the good work," she said, saluting the prize-winner's merit.

Like her, Paula Hacopian and the head of PEPFAR urged Fatou Sylla always to deal with subjects of public interest, in particular those relating to HIV, especially paediatric HIV, which is "a problem in Côte d'Ivoire". "You have our encouragement. We hope for you laurels even better than this one," they said in congratulating the journalist.

The 2024 edition of the Health Awards, coupled with the 21st anniversary of Repmasci, took place on 13 June at the Maison de la presse, in Plateau.

The pieces that caught the jury's attention are entitled "In the difficult daily life of AIDS orphans", produced with the help of Dr Flore Kouassi Lago, Director-Coordinator of the PN-OEV, and an interview with the president of the CCM-CI, concerning the funds allocated to people suffering from this condition.

a190.t:
Election 2026 coverage | Jun 01,2026
Ethiopia’s central bank has set forth an ambitious monetary policy overhaul in an audacious move emblematic of global efforts to rein in economic turmoil.
The changes aim squarely at taming the inflationary beast that has taken root in the aftermath of a two-year war, threatening the country’s economic footing. The war exacerbated Ethiopia’s budget deficit, which increased to 3.4pc of the GDP by 2021/22.
Despite recent signals of progress in inflation control – with June 2023’s year-on-year headline inflation dipping below 30pc for the first time in two years – the problem is far from being addressed. The urgency for intervention is evident, with food inflation remaining high and non-food inflation showing an uptick.
Complex factors drive Ethiopia’s inflation, ranging from supply-side constraints to broader macroeconomic policies. The country’s internal conflicts and a global surge in commodity prices have only added fuel to the inflationary fire. Notably, global oil prices jumped 140pc between mid-2020 and mid-2022.
Efforts to buffer the economy against shocks, like the pandemic and militarised conflicts, led to lax fiscal and monetary policies, which inadvertently worsened inflation. Now, the central bank aims to restore balance. Perhaps for the first time in decades, its officials plan to target inflation, addressing food prices, which constitute 54pc of the Consumer Price Index (CPI). Their latest decision to limit credit growth is seen as both audacious and shrewd, for the Central Bank is not halting credit but aims to manage its expansion more cautiously.
Mamo Mihretu, governor of the National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE), candidly addressed the challenges the economy has been grappling with, particularly the inflation rate, which he admitted was aggravated by “uncharacteristically loose” fiscal and monetary policies over the past two years.
“These were deemed necessary to mitigate the impact of the war, drought, and the massive internal displacement,” the Govenor said in a press conference at the Central Bank’s headquarters on Sudan Street. “But we’re seeing the consequences.”
Yet, the challenges of war and conflicts are not the only culprits. Diminished foreign aid, a budget deficit ballooning to 76.5 billion Br in the third quarter of the fiscal year and exacerbated by global price hikes have all contributed to the turmoil. Governor Mamo rolled out a set of aggressive changes, including capping loans to the federal government at one-third of the current value. It is a bold move, considering the direct advances to the central government had surged by a staggering 91pc at the end of last year, culminating in 159 billion Br.
Fiscal and monetary experts, who have long argued for budget discipline and a tighter monetary stance, met the announcements with approval.
Abdulmenan Mohammed (PhD), a London-based financial analyst, one of the experts pleased with the decision, concurs with a general policy shift towards an interest-based monetary policy framework. He emphasised on political autonomy of the central bank as of first-order importance. Successfully moving past the reserve-prioritising central banking framework requires a simultaneous upgrade to the structural integrity of the institution, according to Abdulmenan.
The mandatory treasury bond purchases of commercial banks imposed by the central bank contradicted a general orientation towards politically independent central banking, he argued.
“The central bank's independence is crucial for its effectiveness,” he told Fortune.
Tewodros Mekonen (PhD), a macroeconomist with ties to the London School of Economics, agrees that abandoning the reserve-based orientation in monetary policy requires credible institutions but asserts that development objectives in a poor country can be calibrated by maintaining the transparency of the central bank despite slight nudges from the government. He characterised the new trajectory of the Central Bank as a hybrid of interest and reserve-based monetary policy frameworks.
“It’s a return to a more sensible, stringent fiscal approach,” Abdulmenan told Fortune. “However, while commendable, aiming for a 20pc inflation rate might be a tad optimistic."
Tewodros echoed this sentiment.
“While the measures are steps in the right direction, the federal government must exercise caution and avoid viewing the central bank as an open treasury,” he told Fortune.
Central Bank’s gross claims (including direct advance and bonds) on the central government stood at 514 billion Br until March, about 48pc higher than the previous year. Direct advances have already reached 80 billion Br until the same period. The Central Bank has set an aggregate credit growth ceiling of 14pc for the year. Meanwhile, Mamo maintained that the rate would not decrease total borrowing but merely keep it from ballooning unnecessarily.
The international community and multilateral financial institutions like the IMF have consistently advocated for a blend of interest and reserve-based monetary policy frameworks for countries like Ethiopia. The recent Central Bank moves seem to respond to these recommendations, hinting at a more significant geopolitical alignment and potential international engagement.
The Central Bank has increased its emergency lending rate to commercial banks by two percentage points to 18pc. A two-pronged approach to curtail inflation with a target of 20pc by the end of 2024 and an ambitious 10pc within the next two years is also in store, while the Governor and his Board, chaired by Girma Biru, opted to redirect the economy towards a focus on price stability, signalling an end to the erstwhile fiscal `loose` approach.
Amid these changes, exporters, crucial economic players, have been handed a lifeline. They must now surrender 50pc of their foreign exchange earnings to the central bank and 10pc to commercial banks. This is a significant drop from the previous 70pc forex surrender requirement, a move hailed mainly by the exporter community.
Sisay Amare, who heads the Ethiopian Pulses, Oilseeds & Spices Processors Exporters Association (EPOSPEO), welcomed the forex adjustment.
“We’ve been advocating for a change in these,” he told Fortune. “This could mean an uptick in our foreign exchange accounts.”
While the Association President recognises the role of a lower retention rate for exporters in declining forex inflow, he disclosed that too much of it would be spent on importing consumption goods.
“Even if the forex surrender rate were zero, the import demand would not be met,” he told Fortune.
Gizat Worku, a leading Ethiopian coffee export business figure, concurred.
“This is an incentivising move,” he said. “We’ve already stored export-ready coffee, promising good revenue ahead of the next harvest season.”
Despite a mix of policies over the decades, Ethiopian coffee exports have quivered around a billion dollars reaching an all-time high last year at 1.4 billion dollars from 300,000tns. Gizat indicated that several levers and gears would need to be tweaked in productivity and efficiency to tackle the forex woes of a country largely reliant on agricultural produce for its forex earnings.
However, both exporters caution against seeing this as a long-term panacea. Ethiopia’s export portfolio, especially its coffee exports, needs a deeper structural revamp to ensure consistent foreign currency inflows.
The Ethiopian banking sector, having ridden a wave of lending, is bracing for these changes. The Central Bank’s decision to limit credit growth and hike interest rates on emergency loans is expected to constrain the money supply in the economy.
As of 2023, a notable growth in loans and advances was recorded, which saw a sharp increase of 35pc, reaching 1.4 trillion Br from one trillion Birr in 2022. The increase in loans and advances coincides with a shift in the type of deposits held by commercial banks. Time deposits saw a 25pc increase, reaching 600 billion Br, suggesting a growing preference for longer-term savings plans. Demand deposits, however, saw moderate growth of 15pc, totalling 400 billion Br. Commercial bank disbursement of new loans had shot up by 30pc last year with 427.9 billion Br in fresh loans.
Tewodros argued that despite credit growth over the years, most funds have been absorbed by the public sector through the state-owned behemoth, the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia (CBE). The share of the private sector in outstanding credit was 868.2 billion Br, which stood at 54.6pc of a whopping 1.5 trillion Br total by the end of last year.
“The private sector has been crowded out of the credit market,” he said while indicating that governments are generally inefficient resource allocators.
Aklilu Wubet, president of Wegagen Bank, is optimistic.
“Inflation has become a formidable challenge for the Ethiopian economy,” he told Fortune. “It’s imperative for banks to rally behind efforts to stabilise our economic landscape.”
Wegagen has been returning in the game, netting half a billion Birr profit last year, registering a 335pc increase from the previous year. Outstanding credit of the banking system (including corporate bonds) increased 23.9pc and reached 1.6 trillion Br last year.
Aklilu had expected the move by the Central Bank to limit credit growth and increase interest rates on emergency loans to limit the money supply in the economy.
“Excess credit might be fueling inflation,” said Aklilu.
But challenges remain. As the banking sector comes to terms with the tighter monetary leash, there is potential for credit rationing and market distortions.
Warns Abdulmenan: “We could see a preference for certain customers, potentially leading to corrupt lending practices.”
Yet, there is a golden thread in this financial tapestry: communication. Governor Mamo’s new direction underscores the importance of transparent communication, bolsters market trust and ensures accountability.
The economist, Tewodros, summed up the sentiment succinctly: “Consistent application of publicly stated policy garners trust in the market.”

স্কাই নিউজ আরাবিয়ার মাল্টিমিডিয়া সাংবাদিক ন্যান্সি তাবেট, আল ইত্তিহাদ নিউজ সেন্টারের সিইও ডঃ হামাদ আল কাবি, কেভিন ওয়াই ব্রাউন, বিষয়বস্তুর প্রধান এবং কৌশলের প্রধান, আফ্রিপডস, অনুপ ওমেনের অংশগ্রহণে অধিবেশনটি পরিচালনা করেন। এডিটর, ক্যাম্পেইন মিডল ইস্ট, এবং এনাস আল রিফাই, ডেপুটি ম্যানেজিং এডিটর, দ্য ন্যাশনাল।
ডঃ হামাদ আল কাবি মধ্যপ্রাচ্যে পডকাস্টিংয়ের বিকাশের বিষয়ে কথা বলেছেন, পশ্চিমা সাংবাদিকতার তুলনায় তুলনামূলকভাবে দেরীতে গ্রহণের কথা উল্লেখ করেছেন, কিন্তু তিনি এর বিশাল প্রভাব স্বীকার করেছেন, এই অঞ্চলের দর্শকদের পরিবর্তনশীল প্রবণতা নিয়ে আলোচনা করেছেন এবং সংক্ষিপ্ত ও আকর্ষণীয় তথ্যের জন্য তাদের অনুসন্ধান করেছেন। , এবং প্রথাগত মিডিয়া তার গুরুত্ব হারানোর ঝুঁকি নির্দেশ করে যদি এটি তাদের পরিবর্তন প্রত্যাশার সাথে খাপ খায় না।
যদিও এনাস আল-রিফাই রেডিওর অব্যাহত প্রভাবকে হাইলাইট করেছেন, যা কয়েক দশক ধরে সাংবাদিকতায় আধিপত্য বিস্তার করেছে, এবং দীর্ঘ-ফর্মের কথোপকথনের ক্রমবর্ধমান জনপ্রিয়তাকে স্পর্শ করেছে, যেখানে শ্রোতারা একাধিক কাজ করার সময় আকর্ষণীয় সংলাপ অনুসরণ করে, তিনি প্রতিধ্বনির বিপদ সম্পর্কে সতর্ক করেছিলেন। চেম্বার, অর্থপূর্ণ এবং ভারসাম্যপূর্ণ কথোপকথনের জন্য দৃষ্টিভঙ্গির বৈচিত্র্যের গুরুত্বের উপর জোর দেয়।
কেভিন ওয়াই ব্রাউন সম্প্রচার থেকে পডকাস্টিং-এ রূপান্তর সম্পর্কে কথা বলেছেন, বিশেষ করে আফ্রিকায়, যেখানে রেডিও এখনও একটি অপরিহার্য ভূমিকা পালন করে, জোর দিয়ে যে পডকাস্টিং শ্রোতাদের যে কোনো সময় তাদের পছন্দের বিষয়বস্তু অ্যাক্সেস করতে নমনীয়তা দেয়, একই সাথে উপস্থাপকদের মধ্যে স্বচ্ছতা এবং আস্থা বাড়ায়। শ্রোতারা, লক্ষ্য করছেন যে পডকাস্ট মতামত এবং প্রতিবেদনের মধ্যে লাইনগুলিকে অস্পষ্ট করেছে এবং ক্রমবর্ধমানভাবে রাজনৈতিক বক্তৃতা এবং জনমতকে আকার দিয়েছে।
অনুপ ওমেন একবিংশ শতাব্দীর গোড়ার দিকে পডকাস্ট বুম এবং সোশ্যাল মিডিয়া প্ল্যাটফর্মের বিপ্লবের মধ্যে একটি তুলনা আঁকেন, তারা কীভাবে বিষয়বস্তু তৈরি এবং ব্যবহারকে রূপান্তরিত করেছে তা তুলে ধরেন, জোর দিয়েছিলেন যে বর্তমান প্রযুক্তি-বুদ্ধিমান শ্রোতারা প্রোগ্রাম প্রদানকারীদের সাথে একটি সংযোগ তৈরি করার প্রত্যাশা করে এবং তাদের দায়বদ্ধ রাখার ক্ষমতা।
ওমেন পডকাস্টের জন্য একটি উজ্জ্বল ভবিষ্যত কল্পনা করেছিল, এটিকে আধুনিক মিডিয়ার ভিত্তি হিসাবে বর্ণনা করে এবং তথ্য, শিক্ষিত এবং অনুপ্রাণিত করার ক্ষমতাকে স্পর্শ করেছিল।
সেশনের অংশগ্রহণকারীরা সাংবাদিকতা এবং জনসাধারণের মিথস্ক্রিয়া বিকাশের জন্য একটি মূল বাহন হিসাবে পডকাস্টের রূপান্তরকারী শক্তির উপর জোর দিয়েছিলেন এবং সম্মত হন যে পডকাস্টগুলি কীভাবে গল্প বলা হয় তা পুনর্নির্মাণ করছে এবং শ্রোতারা কীভাবে সামগ্রী ব্যবহার করে এবং তার সাথে যোগাযোগ করে তাও প্রভাবিত করে৷
(আমি শেষ)

World Media Congress discusses how podcasts are reshaping the media landscape – Federation of OIC News Agencies

The session was moderated with the participation of Nancy Tabet, multimedia journalist at Sky News Arabia; Dr. Hamad Al Kaabi, CEO of Al Ittihad News Center; Kevin Y. Brown, Head of Content and Strategy, Afripods; Anup Oommen, Editor, Campaign Middle East; and Enas Al Rifai, Deputy Managing Editor, The National.

Dr. Hamad Al Kaabi spoke about the development of podcasting in the Middle East, noting its relatively late adoption compared to Western journalism, but he acknowledged its enormous impact, discussed the changing trends of audiences in the region and their search for concise and engaging information, and pointed to the risk of traditional media losing its importance if it does not adapt to their changing expectations.

While Enas Al-Rifai highlighted the continued influence of radio, which has dominated journalism for decades, and touched on the growing popularity of long-form conversations, in which listeners follow engaging dialogue while doing multiple tasks, he warned about the dangers of echo chambers, stressing the importance of diversity of perspectives for meaningful and balanced conversation.

Kevin Y. Brown spoke about the transition from broadcasting to podcasting, particularly in Africa, where radio still plays an indispensable role, emphasising that podcasting gives listeners the flexibility to access their preferred content at any time, while at the same time increasing transparency and trust between presenters and listeners, noting that podcasts have blurred the lines between opinion and reporting and have increasingly shaped political discourse and public opinion.

Anup Oommen drew a comparison between the podcast boom of the early twenty-first century and the revolution of social media platforms, highlighting how they transformed content creation and consumption, and emphasised that today's tech-savvy listeners expect to form a connection with programme providers and to have the power to hold them accountable.

Oommen envisioned a bright future for podcasts, describing them as the foundation of modern media and touching on their power to inform, educate and inspire.

The participants of the session stressed the transformative power of podcasts as a key vehicle for the development of journalism and public interaction, and agreed that podcasts are reshaping how stories are told and are also influencing how listeners consume and interact with content.

(I end)

Building Somalia's Innovation Future Through Intellectual Property
For much of its modern history, Somalia has been a nation of traders, builders, and improvisers. Every Somali marketplace is a living laboratory of ideas: merchants combining supply routes, craftsmen adapting imported tools, and, more recently, young coders experimenting with digital payment systems. Innovation is already embedded in the Somali spirit. What has been missing is the institutional and legal scaffolding to promote it, protect it, refine it, and turn it into an economic value. That scaffolding is what intellectual property (IP) provides.
Why Innovation Matters Now
The world is entering the third industrial revolution—the age of artificial intelligence. The first revolution mechanized production through steam and industry; the second digitized it through computers and the internet. The third, driven by data and algorithms, is transforming how nations produce, trade, and govern.
Yet Somalia has barely benefited from the first two. The machinery of the nineteenth century never took root, and the computer revolution largely passed by a country that remains riddled with conflict and without reliable power, research institutions, or industrial policy. While others debate how to regulate AI or capture its economic potential, Somalia still lacks even the foundations that make innovation possible—education systems, intellectual property protection, and a national innovation strategy.
This is not just a technological lag; it is a structural one. The world is creating wealth from ideas, but Somalia’s economy still depends on livestock, remittances, and humanitarian aid. Youth make up over seventy percent of the population, yet few have access to programs that turn their creativity into products or services. Innovation remains unrecognized, unprotected, and unsupported.
Unless Somalia changes course, it risks missing not just the third industrial revolution but the entire trajectory of modern development. Innovation is no longer a choice; it is the bridge between surviving and belonging in the global economy.
The Intellectual Property Connection [1]
Intellectual property bridges creativity and innovation with capital. It turns abstract ideas into recognizable assets—patents for inventions, trademarks for brands, copyrights for creative works, and industrial designs for craftsmanship. Together, these rights give creators and investors confidence that their effort and risk will be rewarded rather than copied.
By granting the holder the legal right to control the use of their creation—whether to license, commercialize, or exclude competitors—intellectual property transforms imagination into competitive market advantage. It is the mechanism through which ideas become investments and innovation becomes enterprise. Without IP, creativity and innovation remain informal: they circulate through imitation and oral exchange but rarely scale into business. With IP, creativity and innovation gain identity, ownership, and tradable value.
A predictable IP system [2] signals to investors and entrepreneurs that Somalia takes creativity and innovation seriously. It tells young creators that their efforts will be protected and respected, not stolen or diluted. And it tells the international community that Somalia can host technology transfer, joint ventures, and creative industries without fear of legal vacuum. In short, IP is the legal infrastructure of imagination and innovation.
Somalia’s Legal Starting Point
Somalia is not starting from nothing. Before 1991, the country had a functioning IP framework. The Trade Marks Ordinance No. 3 of 1955, [3] later amended by Law No. 33 of 1975 and Law No. 3 of 1987, [4] established a registration system with examination, opposition, and ten-year renewable protection. The Copyright Law No. 66 of 1977 followed the Tunis Model Law, while separate ordinances existed for patents and industrial designs.
After state collapse, these systems went dormant. Only the trade-mark registry survived in fragments and has recently been revived under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry. There is no constitutional reference to IP and, to the writer’s understanding, there is no active patent or copyright office, and no accession to the major WIPO conventions. Yet the surviving trade-mark procedure still bears witness to a legal continuity that can be rebuilt.
From Protection to Productivity
Reactivating old IP laws is not enough; they must be reimagined. Somalia needs a modern system that not only protects ownership but also stimulates creativity. That shift depends on three key policy choices.
First, link protection to productivity. Intellectual property should not exist in isolation from economic activity. Instead of relying on tax incentives—which require fiscal systems Somalia does not yet have—the government can use innovation grants, public procurement preferences, and fast-track registration to reward creativity. For instance, a university start-up developing a solar-powered water pump could receive a grant to scale production or priority access to government contracts.
Second, make access simple and affordable. Current trade-mark fees, designed for foreign applicants, exclude most local entrepreneurs. A tiered fee structure or micro-enterprise waiver would open the system to artisans, start-ups, and youth innovators—the real drivers of job creation. Many developing countries, including Kenya and Rwanda, use such mechanisms to help small inventors and community enterprises enter formal markets.
Third, connect registration with commercialization. Protecting innovation only matters when ideas can reach the market. Somalia should establish Technology and Innovation Support Centers to help inventors move from registration to production. These centers can link innovators with manufacturers, provide technical advice on design and materials, and help ensure compliance with product standards. They can also connect start-ups with investors and industry partners, turning registered ideas into locally made goods. Rwanda’s experience shows that even modest investment in such centers can turn intellectual property from a legal formality into a real engine of manufacturing and growth. For further reading on African innovation and intellectual property experiences, see [5].
How Innovation Feeds Growth and Jobs
The economic chain is quite straightforward. When entrepreneurs invent new products or processes, they raise productivity. Higher productivity leads to competitive pricing and export expansion, which help build enterprises. Expanded exports generate foreign exchange and revenues that fund further development and public services. The ripple continues as industries mature, creating skilled employment and attracting further investment.
Empirical evidence supports this chain. The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) [6] studies show that increase in firm-level innovation spending raises productivity over time. In developing economies, innovation explains a third of GDP growth differences among peers. For youth employment, innovation’s impact is even more direct: each new technology-oriented firm generates about five times more skilled jobs than a traditional trader of equivalent size.
For Somalia, where seventy percent of the population is under thirty, this linkage is decisive. A strong IP system would encourage young entrepreneurs to formalize their ideas, protect them, and attract financing. It would also allow Somali universities and technical institutes to commercialize research, licensing technologies in agriculture, fisheries, and renewable energy.
Somali Fintech Innovation: A Homegrown Revolution
Somalia does not need to look abroad for examples of innovation. Its own telecom and fintech sector tells the story better than any imported model. In a country with no formal banking infrastructure, Somali companies such as Hormuud, Somtel, and Telesom built fully digital payment ecosystems—EVC Plus, E-Dahab, and Zaad—that today process millions of transactions every day. Long before many African governments developed regulatory sandboxes or mobile-money frameworks, Somalia’s private sector had already achieved near-universal adoption of cashless payments.
This achievement rests on ingenuity, not foreign aid. Hormuud, for instance, developed EVC Plus from scratch and upgraded it into a secure, interoperable platform that functions even in areas without internet connectivity. In 2023 it became the first telecom in the Horn of Africa to launch 5G mobile service, deploying local engineering talent and reinvesting domestic revenue. In effect, Somalia leapfrogged traditional development stages—moving from cash to mobile money to 5G in barely two decades.
What is remarkable is that all this happened without an operational IP regime. The absence of patent protection or data regulation did not stop innovation; but it left Somali innovators vulnerable. Their intellectual assets—software architectures, brand identity, and proprietary algorithms—remain largely unprotected beyond company secrecy. As competition intensifies and regional players eye Somalia’s model, the need for formal IP and data-protection frameworks becomes urgent.
The Somali fintech experience makes the lessons unmistakable. Somali creativity shines brightest when it tackles real problems. Private initiative alone cannot sustain success; it needs the protection of law to grow and attract investment. Had a functioning IP system existed when these fintech innovations emerged, Somalia could have exported its technology, licensed its platforms, or attracted joint-venture capital under enforceable agreements.
Hormuud’s 5G launch shows that Somali companies can innovate at a world-class level even in fragile conditions. What they now need is a regulatory and IP environment that rewards their risk-taking, protects their products and brands, and prevents foreign appropriation. Properly designed IP and competition laws would not slow this momentum; they would anchor it—turning Somali innovation from improvisation into enduring advantage.
Youth: The Heart of Innovation
No country builds an innovation economy without its youth. In Somalia, young people are not just a demographic majority—they are the nation’s creative core. They are the programmers who power fintech systems, the artists who redefine cultural expression, and the engineers who improvise tools from discarded metal. Their imagination, more than oil or minerals, is Somalia’s most renewable resource.
But imagination without support evaporates. Somalia’s youth need an environment where creativity meets opportunity. That begins with education that teaches problem-solving rather than rote learning, and access to spaces—incubators, co-working hubs, and online platforms—where ideas can grow. An IP system that recognizes their inventorship and authorship, protects their products, software, music, and designs, and gives them the confidence to seek investors would turn them from job seekers into job creators.
Youth also drive Somalia’s digital economy. Across Somalia, thousands of young developers and designers already freelance for global clients. With an enforceable copyright and digital IP framework, Somalia could formalize this "silent export sector,” allowing youth to earn fair value for their creations while contributing foreign exchange to the economy.
Equally critical is inclusion. Women and rural youth must be part of the innovation story. Making IP accessible through low-cost registration, mentorship, and recognition will become a tool of empowerment. Somalia’s future innovators do not need just inspiration; they need infrastructure and trust. A generation raised in crisis has learned resilience; with law and opportunity on their side, it can now learn prosperity.
So, What Should Somalia Do?
Somalia’s intellectual property reform should begin with a unified and practical registration system encompassing both trademarks and technical innovations. In its initial phase, registration should rely primarily on formal requirements, ensuring prompt recognition of rights—domestic and foreign—without the expense or delay of substantive examination. This approach reflects transitional practices in several jurisdictions that grant protection once filing formalities are satisfied, subject to later challenge. It would give Somali creators and enterprises visible ownership and legal certainty to operate.
As institutional capacity develops, trademark registration can move more quickly toward substantive examination, since assessing distinctiveness and prior use is procedurally straightforward and internationally standardized. Patent protection should progress more gradually. Somalia can introduce utility models to safeguard local innovations and maintain a registration-based patent system for foreign inventions until it acquires the expertise for technical examination. This phased approach combines rapid access to protection with gradual capacity building, aligning early innovation incentives with long-term compliance and credibility.
Building on this foundation, trademark operations should be digitized and linked to customs enforcement to intercept counterfeits, protect consumers, and give Somali products a verifiable commercial identity in regional and international markets. Registration for local entrepreneurs should remain affordable to encourage artisans, micro-enterprises, and start-ups to formalize their brands, while still accommodating foreign firms through direct national filings. That balance—accessible registration for domestic creators and predictable procedures for foreign investors—would strengthen both public confidence and international trust.
For small-scale inventions, utility models offer a practical, low-cost mechanism to protect incremental innovations that do not meet full patent standards. Experiences from other African countries show that such systems draw artisans, engineers, and young innovators into the formal economy. In Somalia, this instrument could recognize the ingenuity of local problem-solvers in agriculture, fisheries, and renewable energy who currently lack access to patent protection.
For foreign applicants, Somalia may initially adopt a registration-based patent system similar to South Africa’s, where rights are granted following a documentary review rather than full technical examination. Under this model, inventions already patented elsewhere could be recorded in Somalia within a defined period that balances filing costs with expected commercial value. This would allow early protection and generate modest state revenue while deferring examination until Somalia joins the Paris or Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) systems. Over time, with support from WIPO and ARIPO, Somalia can establish the human and institutional capacity required for full examination.
All reforms should be anchored in a unified, transparent IP registry that meets WIPO data standards and is accessible online. The existing trademark office could evolve into a one-stop Intellectual Property and Innovation Registry, managing trademarks, utility models, and patent filings, with fee-sharing mechanisms funding examiner training and digital upgrades. A National IP and Innovation Policy should guide this transition by identifying priority sectors—such as creative industries, agriculture, renewable energy, and digital technology—and setting timelines for integration into international frameworks, including the Madrid Protocol, the Paris Convention, the PCT, and ARIPO. Each stage must connect protection with productivity, ensuring that intellectual property becomes a driver of enterprise, investment, and sustainable innovation.
Why Does an IP System Matter in Somalia?
Somalia’s reconstruction has long focused on visible infrastructure. Yet the infrastructure of ideas is just as critical. A functioning intellectual property system that includes accessible utility models and modern registration facilities creates invisible highways for innovation. It reassures investors that Somalia is open for lawful business and reassures citizens that their ideas belong to them.
In a region where foreign companies increasingly seek local partners, such credibility is invaluable. Investors are rarely deterred by risk; they are almost always deterred by uncertainty. A transparent IP registry with clear procedures and public ownership records is the antidote to that uncertainty. It can transform Somalia from a consumer of innovation into a co-creator within regional and global value chains.
Innovation turns dependence into dignity. When a Somali start-up registers a utility model for an irrigation system or a software firm licenses code abroad, it shows that creativity itself is a national export. That is the essence of modern sovereignty—the capacity to create and protect ideas, not merely to defend borders.
Conclusion
Somalia’s innovation future will not be built overnight, but it can begin now—with pragmatic reforms that transform intellectual property from a colonial relic into a national growth engine. The 1955 Trade Marks Ordinance gave Somalia a legal foundation; a new generation of utility models, design rights, and innovation-friendly registration systems can give it purpose.
If designed with inclusion, transparency, and credibility, these tools can attract investors, empower youth, and make the law an ally of imagination. Properly used, intellectual property can become Somalia’s quiet revolution—a bridge between creativity and capital, and between survival and prosperity.
References and Notes
[1] Intellectual property does not exist in isolation. Laws can protect ideas, but they cannot create them. Innovation depends on the strength of a nation’s education, research, finance, governance, and infrastructure systems. Somalia’s ability to turn protection into productivity will therefore hinge on the growth of human capital, the credibility of its institutions, access to finance, and the reliability of its infrastructure. While a full analysis of these broader conditions lies beyond the scope of this essay, they form the essential context in which Somalia’s intellectual property reforms must take root.
[2] A functioning IP regime is only as strong as the environment around it. Entrepreneurs and foreign investors need a legal system that guarantees fairness and predictability. Courts play a central role in this ecosystem—not only by enforcing contracts but by ensuring that rights are applied consistently and disputes are resolved transparently. When laws are applied predictably, investors and innovators gain the confidence to take risks.
[3] www.somalilandlaw.com, last visited October 18, 2025.
[4] https://intellectual-property-helpdesk.ec.europa.eu/document/download/321a7f9c-5e4a-49db-83d4-b18e021804e6_en?filename=IP+SOMALIA+FINAL.pdf, last visited October 18, 2025.
[5] https://rdb.rw/neworg1/intellectual-property-rights/, Last visited October 17, 2025. https://www.wipo.int/web-publications/global-innovation-index-2025/en/gii-2025-results.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com, last visited October 16, 2025. SUMMARY-Mapping Innovation Report.pdf, last visited October 12, 2025. SME and Entrepreneurship Policy in Egypt: SME and Entrepreneurship Programmes in Egypt | OECD, last visited October 18, 2025. Egypt Establishes a New Authority for Intellectual Property - riad-riad.com, last visited October 20, 2025. wipo_casestudy_ip_comm_za.pdf, last visited October 20, 2025.
[6] OECD is composed mainly of developed economies, with South Africa serving as its only African Key Partner. Other African countries, including Egypt, Kenya, and Rwanda, engage through structured cooperation programs rather than full membership. Egypt participates in a three-year OECD Country Programme supporting governance and economic reforms; Kenya collaborates under the Inclusive Framework on Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS); and Rwanda is a member of the OECD Development Centre, which connects developing economies to OECD research and policy dialogue.
About the Author
The writer holds a Ph.D. from Georgetown University (Washington, DC), a Juris Doctorate from Georgia State University (Atlanta, GA) and a Laurea from Somali National University (Gahayr Campus). He has practiced law for more than twenty years, including over two decades in the United States, where he was an intellectual property lawyer and partner in both medium-sized IP boutiques of 100–200 lawyers and large general-practice firms with more than 800 lawyers. Holding a PhD in organic chemistry, he has had a distinguished career helping pharmaceutical and chemical companies protect their innovations in medicine—including cancer, pain, and genetic (CRISPR-type) therapies—as well as in formulations, synthetic materials, fine chemicals and agrochemicals such as insecticides, herbicides, and fungicides. Over the course of his career, he has prosecuted hundreds of patent applications through the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office and in foreign jurisdictions including the European Patent Office, China, Japan, India, Brazil, and South Africa. He has advised innovative pharmaceutical companies on maximizing protection for branded medicines during regulatory approval and represented generic manufacturers seeking to bring affordable new therapies to market. More recently, he has contributed to the development of Somalia’s National Export Promotion Strategy and helped draft key trade legislation. He has also provided legal analysis on Somalia’s pathway to integration into the East African Community (EAC) Treaty, focusing on the legal and institutional reforms required to comply with the Treaty’s obligations.
