Il faut, cependant, souligner la convergence de vue avec l’ensemble des acteurs du secteur minier. En effet, plusieurs entreprises minières, après des négociations, s’apprêtent à migrer sur le code de 2023 et elles s’engagent toutes à appliquer les mesures du contenu local.
L’Essor : Aux yeux de nombreux Maliens, la Société de recherche et d’exploitation des ressources minérales du Mali (SOREM) connaît un démarrage timide. Que faut-il aujourd’hui pour rendre cette structure véritablement opérationnelle ?
Pr Amadou Keïta : C’est un constat qui ne prend pas toujours en compte le contexte dans sa globalité et les actions en cours pour permettre à la Sorem de faire face aux défis du moment. En effet, la société d’État SOREM, créée en août 2022, porte en elle une volonté affirmée du président de la Transition, le colonel Assimi Goïta, de remettre l’État au cœur du système de recherche, d’exploitation et de commercialisation des produits miniers.
Son opérationnalisation est l’une des priorités du département des Mines. Cette société a tenu la 2ème session de son conseil d’administration le 25 juillet 2024 et vient de se voir attribuer par le Conseil des ministres un permis de recherche d’or sur le périmètre de N’Tahaka d’une superficie de 97,41 km², dans le Cercle de N’Tillit à Gao. Les données recueillies suite aux travaux de recherche géologique et minière exécutés dans le district géologique du Gourma oriental, nous ont permis de mettre en évidence plusieurs secteurs d’intérêt potentiel dont celui de N’Tahaka et la SOREM est déjà engagée à approfondir l’exploration en vue d’une exploitation prochaine des richesses du sous-sol au bénéfice des peuples du Mali. Elle s’active, également, depuis quelques semaines à un positionnement stratégique sur les mines en difficultés dans notre pays. C’est le cas de la mine de Morila qui reviendra sous la coupe de la SOREM afin de s’assurer de la continuité de son exploitation après les moments difficiles que la mine a connus du fait de l’indélicatesse de son précédent opérateur. Les autres actifs miniers appartenant à cette société australienne reviendront également à la SOREM. L’État entend apporter les moyens utiles et adéquats à la SOREM pour mener à bien sa mission.
L’Essor : Où en êtes-vous avec le projet d’installation de l’usine d’affinage d’or ?
Pr Amadou Keïta : Ce projet est une des dimensions du partenariat que nous avons avec la Russie dans le secteur minier et il se présente comme un tournant décisif dans l’organisation et la gestion de ce secteur. Vous n’êtes pas sans savoir que l’objectif final de ce processus est que tout l’or produit sur le territoire du Mali soit raffiné au Mali dans des conditions optimales.
C’est un processus qui évolue bien et demande une coopération intense à plusieurs niveaux. L’État a mis à la disposition de ce projet d’usine d’affinage un espace de 10 hectares et dispose d’un plan de conception sommaire de l’unité. Le cahier de charges ainsi que les éléments nécessaires pour la conduite d’une étude de faisabilité sont disponibles.
Un suivi régulier est fait avec le partenaire russe pour que notre pays dispose, après un peu plus de 60 ans d’exploitation de l’or, d’une usine d’affinage répondant aux standards internationaux.
L’Essor : La renégociation du contrat de lithium de Goulamina a permis de porter la participation de l’État et des nationaux à 35% contre 20% précédemment. Que représente cette part en termes de ressources pour les caisses publiques ?
Pr Amadou Keïta : Je voudrais d’abord féliciter le gouvernement du Mali pour cet accord et pour le projet de la mine de lithium de Goulamina, l’un des plus grands projets de lithium en Afrique et dans le monde. Il reflète la politique de diversification que nous prônons dans l’exploitation des ressources minérales de notre pays.
Pour revenir à votre question, il est important de voir au-delà des pourcentages énoncés qui concernent, uniquement, l’apport direct du secteur minier, en termes de dividendes, à l’État et aux nationaux qui seront actionnaires. À ce niveau, une première estimation fait état d’une augmentation du budget de l’État à hauteur d’environ 100 milliards de Fcfa par an. Mais, je voudrais faire noter que ce projet de la mine de lithium de Goulamina aura des apports sous d’autres formes qui permettront une contribution additionnelle significative au financement du développement des secteurs minier et énergétique, du secteur des infrastructures et des transports, en plus du développement local. Il est attendu, par exemple, un minimum de 250 milliards de Fcfa de chiffres d’affaires pour les entreprises locales sous-traitantes et une création d’emplois considérable dans la région de Bougouni.
Je rappelle également que cette mine est opérée par le partenaire Chinois Ganfeng Lithium Co, l’un des plus grands producteurs de lithium, de batteries de lithium et de produits dérivés de lithium. Ainsi donc grâce à ce projet, le Mali mettra en place une usine de spodumène qui démarrera sa production avant la fin de l’année 2024. Ce sont donc des milliers d’emplois créés en perspective et le développement de toutes les zones riveraines du projet.
L’Essor : L’État a-t-il les moyens d’être présent à tous les niveaux de la chaîne d’exploitation pour pouvoir déterminer la rentabilité réelle de cette mine de lithium ?
Pr Amadou Keïta : C’est un chantier qui s’étend, pour nous, à l’ensemble des sociétés minières qui opèrent au Mali. L’administration minière a cette obligation de veiller à une exploitation juste de nos ressources et le nouveau code minier renvoie l’ensemble des services du Ministère des mines et d’autres départements ministériels à un contrôle strict de l’activité minière sur notre territoire.
Notre État doit, dès lors, se donner les moyens pour parvenir à un suivi des sociétés minières autant sur la valeur réelle des exportations que sur le respect de toutes les dispositions de leurs activités notamment les normes environnementales en vigueur. C’est tout le sens de la réforme institutionnelle que nous engageons pour permettre à nos services d’être à même de répondre à cette donne importante pour notre pays.
L’Essor : Peut-on alors considérer que la signature, par le Premier ministre, du décret portant annulation du permis d’exploitation de la mine de manganèse à Tassiga, est un des effets de ces réformes ?
Pr Amadou Keïta : Je voudrais d’emblée dire que notre objectif n’est pas de procéder à des annulations de titres miniers. Cela installe des périodes d’incertitudes pour la chaîne de valeur de la mine, des travailleurs aux entreprises sous-traitantes, en passant par les communautés riveraines.
Mais, en tout état de cause, la responsabilité nous incombe de veiller au respect des lois en vigueur en République du Mali. Dès lors, quand les conditions sont réunies pour faire constater des manquements graves dans la convention qui lie l’État à la société minière, nous sommes appelés à faire appliquer la loi dans toute sa rigueur.
Sur la mine de manganèse de Tassiga, attribuée à la société Metal Mass PTY Ltd depuis juillet 2011, notre administration a relevé des faits dont certains appelaient une annulation immédiate et sans mise en demeure du permis. Dans ce cas précis, nous entendons faire prévaloir les intérêts de l’État et de nos populations.
L’Essor : Des informations ont fait état de l’exportation frauduleuse d’importantes quantités d’or. L’État peine également à recouvrer la totalité de ses gains auprès des sociétés minières. Quel mécanisme envisagez-vous pour minimiser les pertes ?
Pr Amadou Keïta : Les régimes d’exploitation de l’or au Mali sont au nombre de trois suivant les dispositions du Code minier. La grande mine, la petite mine et l’exploitation artisanale de l’or. Toute exploitation qui se ferait en dehors de ce cadre est illégale et les dispositions du code minier sont très précises sur les sanctions auxquelles s’exposent les personnes ou les sociétés qui se livreraient à une exploitation illégale.
Je dois préciser que notre dispositif se renforce avec la perspective de création d’une brigade spéciale des mines et d’un Commissariat chargé des activités minières. Ces deux organes auront pour mission de mener la répression des infractions à la législation minière. Un troisième organe dédié à l’encadrement et la surveillance des exploitations minières artisanales sera également créé.
C’est la somme d’intervention de toutes ces structures qui devra nous permettre d’améliorer la surveillance du secteur minier et défendre au mieux les intérêts du peuple malien.
Je voudrais réitérer le plein engagement du gouvernement à assainir le secteur minier, par une révision en profondeur du cadastre minier mais aussi par un travail collégial de contrôle et de répression, le cas échéant.
L’Essor : Quelles sont les grandes actions en perspective dans le secteur minier ?
Pr Amadou Keïta : Nous avons besoin de compléter l’esprit de la réforme du secteur minier par un redimensionnement de certains services du ministère des Mines, à commencer par la Direction nationale de géologie et des Mines (DNGM) afin de leur donner le corpus nécessaire aux innovations apportées par le Code minier de 2023 et la loi relative au contenu local dans le secteur minier.
Au-delà, nous restons pleinement engagés dans la complète mise en route de la Sorem qui se concrétisera par la reprise prochaine des activités de la mine de Morila et par le démarrage des activités d’exploration à N’Tahaka. Dans la même foulée, nous maintiendrons le suivi rapproché des mines en difficulté pour préserver les emplois et assurer une production optimale d’ensemble.
ID (AMAP)
a1825.en:
Bamako, 1 October (AMAP) – The reform efforts in the mining sector are moving forward. Several mining companies are preparing to migrate to the 2023 code and they are all committing to apply the local content measures. In addition, our framework is being strengthened with the prospect of creating a special mining brigade and a police commission responsible for mining activities. This information was provided by the Minister of Mines, Prof. Amadou Keïta, in this exclusive interview.

L'Essor: What can be concluded about the implementation of the new mining code and of the local content law, one year after their adoption?

Prof. Amadou Keïta: In 2023 our country chose to adopt a new mining code and, for the first time in our history, a law on local content. These are major reforms that are part of an overall vision of the refoundation of our State. These two texts stem from a strong aspiration of the Malian people expressed during the National Refoundation Conference and were designed to bring a new Malian perspective to the management of mineral resources.

It is therefore a reform that raises great hope and that commits us, as the administration in charge of Mines, to work to make them applicable. It is in this spirit that, in July 2024, the implementing decrees of the Mining Code and of the law on local content in the mining sector were adopted. That is to say that the time has not yet come to draw up an assessment of the implementation of these new provisions, but we hope that when they are applied in their full scope, Mali will be able to pride itself on a mining sector fully integrated into the national economy and capable of driving development.

It should nevertheless be stressed that there is a convergence of views with all the actors of the mining sector. Indeed, several mining companies, after negotiations, are preparing to migrate to the 2023 code and they are all committing to apply the local content measures.

L'Essor: In the eyes of many Malians, the Mali Mineral Resources Research and Exploitation Company (SOREM) has got off to a slow start. What is needed today to make this entity truly operational?

Prof. Amadou Keïta: That is an observation that does not always take the overall context into account, nor the actions under way to allow SOREM to face the challenges of the moment. Indeed, the state-owned company SOREM, created in August 2022, embodies the firm determination of the President of the Transition, Colonel Assimi Goïta, to put the State back at the heart of the system of research, exploitation and marketing of mining products.

Making it operational is one of the priorities of the Ministry of Mines. This company held the second session of its board of directors on 25 July 2024 and has just been granted by the Council of Ministers a gold exploration permit over the N'Tahaka perimeter, covering an area of 97.41 km², in the N'Tillit Circle in Gao. The data gathered from the geological and mining research work carried out in the eastern Gourma geological district enabled us to identify several sectors of potential interest, including that of N'Tahaka, and SOREM is already committed to deepening exploration with a view to the forthcoming exploitation of the riches of the subsoil for the benefit of the peoples of Mali. It has also been working for some weeks on a strategic positioning with regard to the mines in difficulty in our country. That is the case of the Morila mine, which will come back under SOREM's control in order to ensure the continuity of its operation after the difficult times the mine went through because of the misconduct of its previous operator. The other mining assets belonging to that Australian company will also revert to SOREM. The State intends to provide SOREM with the useful and adequate resources to carry out its mission.

L'Essor: Where do things stand with the project to install a gold refinery?

Prof. Amadou Keïta: This project is one of the dimensions of the partnership we have with Russia in the mining sector and it represents a decisive turning point in the organisation and management of this sector. You are surely aware that the final objective of this process is that all the gold produced on the territory of Mali be refined in Mali under optimal conditions.

It is a process that is progressing well and that requires intense cooperation at several levels. The State has made available to this refinery project an area of 10 hectares and has a preliminary design plan for the unit. The specifications as well as the elements necessary for conducting a feasibility study are available.

Regular follow-up is carried out with the Russian partner so that our country may have, after a little more than 60 years of gold mining, a refinery meeting international standards.

L'Essor: The renegotiation of the Goulamina lithium contract made it possible to raise the participation of the State and of nationals to 35%, compared with 20% previously. What does this share represent in terms of resources for the public purse?

Prof. Amadou Keïta: First of all I would like to congratulate the government of Mali for this agreement and for the Goulamina lithium mine project, one of the biggest lithium projects in Africa and in the world. It reflects the diversification policy that we advocate in the exploitation of our country's mineral resources.

To come back to your question, it is important to look beyond the percentages mentioned, which concern only the direct contribution of the mining sector, in terms of dividends, to the State and to the nationals who will be shareholders. At that level, a first estimate points to an increase in the State budget of around 100 billion CFA francs per year. But I would like to note that this Goulamina lithium mine project will bring contributions in other forms that will allow a significant additional contribution to financing the development of the mining and energy sectors, of the infrastructure and transport sector, in addition to local development. For example, a minimum of 250 billion CFA francs in turnover is expected for local subcontracting companies, and considerable job creation in the Bougouni region.

I also recall that this mine is operated by the Chinese partner Ganfeng Lithium Co, one of the largest producers of lithium, lithium batteries and lithium-derived products. Thus, thanks to this project, Mali will set up a spodumene plant that will begin production before the end of 2024. Thousands of jobs are therefore expected to be created, along with the development of all the areas bordering the project.

L'Essor: Does the State have the means to be present at all levels of the exploitation chain in order to determine the real profitability of this lithium mine?

Prof. Amadou Keïta: For us, this is an undertaking that extends to all the mining companies operating in Mali. The mining administration has the obligation to ensure a fair exploitation of our resources, and the new mining code directs all the services of the Ministry of Mines and of other ministerial departments to a strict control of mining activity on our territory.

Our State must therefore give itself the means to achieve a monitoring of mining companies, both on the real value of exports and on compliance with all the provisions governing their activities, in particular the environmental standards in force. That is the whole meaning of the institutional reform we are undertaking to enable our services to be able to respond to this important matter for our country.

L'Essor: Can we then consider that the signing, by the Prime Minister, of the decree cancelling the exploitation permit of the manganese mine at Tassiga is one of the effects of these reforms?

Prof. Amadou Keïta: I would like to say from the outset that our objective is not to proceed with cancellations of mining titles. That creates periods of uncertainty for the mine's value chain, from the workers to the subcontracting companies, including the neighbouring communities.

But in any event, the responsibility falls to us to ensure compliance with the laws in force in the Republic of Mali. Therefore, when the conditions are met to establish serious breaches in the agreement binding the State to the mining company, we are called upon to apply the law in all its rigour.

On the Tassiga manganese mine, awarded to the company Metal Mass PTY Ltd since July 2011, our administration identified facts, some of which called for an immediate cancellation of the permit without formal notice. In this specific case, we intend to uphold the interests of the State and of our people.

L'Essor: Reports have indicated the fraudulent export of large quantities of gold. The State is also struggling to recover all of its earnings from mining companies. What mechanism do you envisage to minimise the losses?

Prof. Amadou Keïta: There are three regimes of gold exploitation in Mali under the provisions of the Mining Code: large-scale mining, small-scale mining and artisanal gold mining. Any exploitation carried out outside this framework is illegal, and the provisions of the mining code are very precise on the penalties faced by persons or companies engaging in illegal exploitation.

I must specify that our framework is being strengthened with the prospect of creating a special mining brigade and a Police Commission responsible for mining activities. These two bodies will have the mission of carrying out the repression of violations of mining legislation. A third body dedicated to the supervision and monitoring of artisanal mining operations will also be created.

It is the combined intervention of all these structures that should enable us to improve the surveillance of the mining sector and to defend as well as possible the interests of the Malian people.

I would like to reiterate the government's full commitment to cleaning up the mining sector, through an in-depth review of the mining cadastre but also through collegial work of control and, where appropriate, enforcement.

L'Essor: What are the major actions in prospect in the mining sector?

Prof. Amadou Keïta: We need to complete the spirit of the mining sector reform with a resizing of certain services of the Ministry of Mines, beginning with the National Directorate of Geology and Mines (DNGM), in order to give them the body of resources required by the innovations introduced by the 2023 Mining Code and the law on local content in the mining sector.

Beyond that, we remain fully committed to the complete launch of SOREM, which will take concrete form through the forthcoming resumption of activities at the Morila mine and through the start of exploration activities at N'Tahaka. In the same vein, we will maintain close monitoring of the mines in difficulty in order to preserve jobs and ensure optimal overall production.

ID (AMAP)

a1877.t:
The African Guarantee Fund (AGF) today announced the launch of its Mission 300 Local Currency Guarantee Facility, a groundbreaking initiative to mobilize $5 billion to support energy access projects across Africa. This facility targets financing for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the Distributed Renewable Energy (DRE) sector.
The facility forms a critical component of an ambitious initiative led by the African Development Bank Group and the World Bank Group to provide electricity to 300 million Africans by 2030.
Africa faces a significant energy access challenge, with approximately 600 million people lacking electricity as of 2023. The continent is estimated to require an annual investment of nearly $25 billion to achieve universal energy access by 2030.
“The Mission 300 Local Currency Guarantee Facility will encourage collaboration with African governments whilst leveraging concessional financing from the African Development Bank, the World Bank Group, and other development partners to scale the involvement of local banks in financing Distributed Renewable Energy solutions,” said Wale Shonibare, Director for Energy Financial Solutions, Policy and Regulations at the African Development Bank. He is also a Non-Executive Director with the Africa Guarantee Fund.
The fund has been at the forefront of bridging the financing gap facing green SMEs by steering the implementation of the Green Guarantee Facility, supported by the Nordic Development Fund and the Investment Fund for Developing Countries.
The Green Guarantee Facility has mobilized financing for green, clean, and renewable energy projects while positioning AGF as a leader in driving sustainable development in Africa. The Green Guarantee Facility mitigates risks within loan portfolios, lowering the exposure of financial institutions to defaults and enhancing their confidence in lending to distributed renewable energy SMEs. It has also accelerated electrification efforts, particularly in underserved rural and peri-urban communities.
By addressing systemic barriers such as high collateral requirements, currency mismatches, and the lack of long-term financing, AGF has been able to de-risk SME lending and mobilize significant private sector capital into Africa’s energy transition.
With its proven track record in catalyzing SME financing while leveraging innovative guarantee solutions and capacity-building programs, the AGF is best positioned to advance Africa’s energy transformation.
“AGF’s leadership in driving financial innovation for SMEs aligns seamlessly with the goals of Mission 300. By addressing financing gaps and fostering public-private partnerships, AGF plays a crucial role in driving inclusive energy solutions, accelerating the energy transition, and reducing carbon emissions across the continent,” said Jules Ngankam, AGF Group CEO. “We have successfully implemented the Green Guarantee, which has facilitated progress toward national commitments under the Africa Energy Declaration, the African Union’s Vision 2063, and the global Sustainable Development Goals, fostering inclusive growth and climate resilience.”
A recent example of AGF’s impact in the energy sector is its participation in a credit guarantee syndication for a 40 MW solar plant in Madagascar. This landmark transaction demonstrated the viability of local currency financing for renewable energy projects in the country while enhancing power sector resilience through diversification away from thermal power. The project, which provides improved electricity access to approximately 285,000 people, supports both UN Sustainable Development Goal 7 (affordable and clean energy) and Goal 13 (climate action) by reducing emissions by 34,000 tonnes of CO2 through the displacement of thermal power.
About Mission 300
Mission 300 is a transformative initiative launched jointly by the African Development Bank and the World Bank Group to accelerate access to clean and sustainable energy for 300 million Africans by 2030. Mission 300 addresses Africa’s significant energy access gap, where nearly 600 million people remain without electricity. Through strategic partnerships, innovative financing mechanisms, and capacity-building efforts, Mission 300 is unlocking private-sector investment to drive the development of distributed renewable energy (DRE) solutions.
By leveraging de-risking tools and aligning with global sustainable development goals, Mission 300 is committed to fostering inclusive growth, enhancing energy security, and building climate resilience across the African continent.
About African Guarantee Fund
African Guarantee Fund, rated AA- by Fitch Ratings, is a specialized guarantee provider whose mission is to facilitate economic development and poverty reduction in Africa. To achieve this, AGF increases access to finance for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) across key economic sectors through an array of guarantee products and capacity development assistance. Since its inception, AGF has unlocked more than $5 billion in SME financing through partnerships with 250 partner financial institutions across 44 African countries.
AGF is backed by the following shareholders and sponsors: The Government of Denmark through the Danish International Development Agency, the Government of Spain through the Spanish Agency for International Cooperation, the African Development Bank, French Development Agency, Nordic Development Fund, Investment Fund for Developing Countries (IFU), German Development Bank, French Agency for Private Sector (PROPARCO), West African Development Bank, Global Affairs Canada, USAID’s West Africa Trade and Investment Hub, TechnoServe, NORAD and Mastercard Foundation.

a1940.t:
Thursday February 6, 2025
Hargeisa (HOL) – British MP Sir Gavin Williamson has renewed calls for the United States to recognize Somaliland following his accusations that the Somali government has misused USAID funds to support Al-Shabaab militants.  
In a statement on X (formerly Twitter) on Sunday, Williamson welcomed the US decision to suspend USAID funding, claiming that Somali authorities were channeling funds to the militant group. 
Williamson also commented on the recent US airstrikes targeting ISIS militants in Puntland, commending the move and calling for a shift in US policy.
"Somalia, through Al-Shabaab, has been sending arms and resources to the Houthis. Donald Trump was right to strike Somalia. Now is the time to recognize Somaliland, the one democratic nation in the region, and stop propping up the terrorist-supporting Mogadishu regime with US dollars," he added.  
However, Hiiraan Online could not independently verify Williamson's allegations regarding the Somali government's involvement in funding Al-Shabaab and the Houthis in Yemen.  
The US military strikes, which occurred on Saturday in the Golis Mountains, killed several ISIS operatives. The Somali president's office said President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud was informed of the airstrike, and he wrote on X that he extended his deepest gratitude for "the unwavering support of the United States in our shared fight against terrorism."
"Your bold and decisive leadership, Mr. President, in counterterrorism efforts is highly valued and welcomed in Somalia.
Williamson, a Conservative Party MP, has long advocated for Somaliland's recognition, frequently raising the issue in the UK Parliament. He has also visited Hargeisa several times during his tenure as the UK's Defense Secretary.

a2058.t:
Élevé au grade d'officier de l'ordre national du Mali Mangal Traoré célébré par les siens :
La jeunesse de l'Association Yirwal Mopti (qui regroupe les ressortissants de la Commune urbaine de Mopti résidant à Bamako ) a organisé le samedi dernier une cérémonie d'hommage à son président Mangal Traoré élevé par le président de la Transition le Général d'armée Assimi Goïta au grade d'Officier de l'ordre national du Mali pour services rendus à la Nation.
L’'événement s'est déroulé au siège de ladite association à Banankabougou en présence des parents, amis, collaborateurs et surtout de nombreuses personnalités constituées d'anciens ministres, de hauts cadres de l'Etat tous natifs de Mopti ou de la Région.Intégrité, honnêteté, humilité, loyauté, respect de la parole donnée... Ce sont les mots qui revenaient lors du déjeuner organisé le samedi 11 octobre 2025 par   la jeunesse de Yiriwal Mopti  pour  féliciter Mangal Traoré rédacteur du projet du nouveau Code de procédure pénale élevé le 22 septembre 2025 au grade d'Officier  de l'Ordre national du Mali par le président de la Transition   le   général   d'Armée   Assimi   Goïta   pour   services rendus à la Nation.  
Les nombreux témoignages rendus au brillant parcours professionnel de Mangal Traoré illustrent la grandeur et la simplicité de l'homme. " Aux côtés du président ATT, Mangal était plus puissant que des ministres mais malgré tout, il est resté lui-même ", a soutenu l'ancien ministre Harouna Cissé. Même témoignage chez un autre ancien ministre qui est aussi un des  présidents d'honneur de Yiriwal,  Hamadoun Touré.
"Ce qui m'a le plus impressionné chez Mangal, c'est son efficacité au travail qui est comparable à une montre Suisse et sa discrétion à l'image d'une tombe. Il a des vertus qui sont de nos jours très rares dans l'administration en Afrique ", a témoigné Touré.
Du premier vice-président de Yirwal Mopti Ibrahim Diallo dit Number au président de l'Association Ginna Dogon et ancien Président de la Cour Suprême, Nouhoum Tapily tous ont salué et félicité l'heureux récipiendaire pour cette distinction.
"Notre fierté, c'est surtout par le fait qu'il a eu cette médaille non pas avec ATT auprès de qui, il a longuement servi mais plutôt sous l'actuel régime. Cela dénote que c'est son mérite, son abnégation qui ont été mis au devant ", a témoigné un ressortissant de la région de Mopti. 
Magistrat de grade exceptionnel, major de promotion
Magistrat de grade exceptionnel, Mangal Traoré est diplômé de l'Ecole nationale d'administration du Mali, major de la promotion Sciences juridiques (1981-1985), diplômé de l'Institut national de formation judiciaire, option magistrature (décembre 1987) et titulaire de plusieurs certificats de formation portant notamment sur la Justice militaire, la lutte contre le terrorisme, la légistique...
Il a entamé sa carrière en qualité de Substitut du procureur de la République près le tribunal de Première Instance de Kayes (1989-1993) et fut successivement Conseiller technique au Ministère de la justice (1995-1998) ; Coordonnateur du Comité de pilotage du programme décennal de développement de la Justice CP-PRODEJ (1998-2000) qui a organisé le Forum national sur la justice en 1999.
Il a été membre du Comité de rédaction du Code de justice militaire en 1995 ; membre des Commissions de relecture du Code pénal et du Code de procédure pénale en 1995 et 2001 ; Rapporteur de la Commission de relecture du Code de procédure pénale en 2001.Il a aussi enseigné la procédure pénale à l'Ecole Nationale d'Administration à plusieurs générations de cadres qui sont aujourd'hui dans toutes les sphères de l'administration, de la justice, de la diplomatie…
 Il a été par la suite Chef du Secrétariat particulier du président de la République (2002-2011), puis Consul général du Mali à Paris (2011 -2015).
Depuis son retour au pays, il a essentiellement travaillé avec des Partenaires techniques et financiers intervenant dans le secteur de la Justice (USAID, PAJM de l'Union Européenne, PNUD…). Outre le Code de procédure pénale, il a aussi assuré en 2017 l'élaboration du projet  de texte portant Statut de la magistrature entré en vigueur en août 2024.Il est fortement impliqué dans les initiatives de développement local concernant sa ville natale, ce qui lui a valu d'être porté à la tête de YIRWAL Mopti en 2018.  
K.THERA
a2058.en:
Raised to the rank of Officer of the National Order of Mali, Mangal Traoré celebrated by his own:

The youth of the Yirwal Mopti Association (which brings together natives of the urban Commune of Mopti living in Bamako) organised last Saturday a tribute ceremony for its president Mangal Traoré, who was raised by the President of the Transition, Army General Assimi Goïta, to the rank of Officer of the National Order of Mali for services rendered to the Nation.

The event took place at the headquarters of the said association in Banankabougou in the presence of relatives, friends, colleagues and above all numerous public figures, made up of former ministers and senior state officials, all natives of Mopti or of the Region. Integrity, honesty, humility, loyalty, respect for one's given word... These are the words that kept coming up during the lunch organised on Saturday 11 October 2025 by the youth of Yiriwal Mopti to congratulate Mangal Traoré, drafter of the bill for the new Code of Criminal Procedure, who was raised on 22 September 2025 to the rank of Officer of the National Order of Mali by the President of the Transition, Army General Assimi Goïta, for services rendered to the Nation.

The numerous testimonies paid to Mangal Traoré's brilliant professional career illustrate the greatness and the simplicity of the man. “Alongside President ATT, Mangal was more powerful than ministers but despite all that, he remained himself,” maintained the former minister Harouna Cissé. The same testimony came from another former minister who is also one of the honorary presidents of Yiriwal, Hamadoun Touré.

“What impressed me most about Mangal is his efficiency at work, which is comparable to a Swiss watch, and his discretion, like that of a grave. He has virtues that are nowadays very rare in the administration in Africa,” testified Touré.

From the first vice-president of Yirwal Mopti, Ibrahim Diallo known as Number, to the president of the Ginna Dogon Association and former President of the Supreme Court, Nouhoum Tapily, all hailed and congratulated the happy recipient on this distinction.

“Our pride comes above all from the fact that he received this medal not under ATT, whom he served for a long time, but rather under the current regime. That shows that it is his merit, his self-denial, that have been put to the fore,” testified a native of the Mopti region.

Magistrate of exceptional rank, top of his class

A magistrate of exceptional rank, Mangal Traoré is a graduate of the National School of Administration of Mali, top of the Legal Sciences class (1981-1985), a graduate of the National Institute of Judicial Training, magistracy option (December 1987), and holder of several training certificates covering in particular military justice, counter-terrorism and legislative drafting.

He began his career as Deputy Public Prosecutor at the Court of First Instance of Kayes (1989-1993) and was successively Technical Adviser at the Ministry of Justice (1995-1998); Coordinator of the Steering Committee of the ten-year programme for the development of Justice, CP-PRODEJ (1998-2000), which organised the National Forum on Justice in 1999.

He was a member of the Drafting Committee of the Code of Military Justice in 1995; a member of the Commissions for the review of the Penal Code and the Code of Criminal Procedure in 1995 and 2001; Rapporteur of the Commission for the review of the Code of Criminal Procedure in 2001. He also taught criminal procedure at the National School of Administration to several generations of officials who are today in all spheres of the administration, of the judiciary, of diplomacy...

He was subsequently Head of the Private Secretariat of the President of the Republic (2002-2011), then Consul General of Mali in Paris (2011-2015).

Since his return to the country, he has essentially worked with technical and financial partners operating in the Justice sector (USAID, the European Union's PAJM, UNDP...). Besides the Code of Criminal Procedure, he also ensured in 2017 the drafting of the bill on the Statute of the Magistracy, which came into force in August 2024. He is strongly involved in local development initiatives concerning his home town, which earned him being placed at the head of YIRWAL Mopti in 2018.

K. THERA

a2133.t:
MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somalia’s government on Tuesday dismissed Arab Dheg Ahmed, the commander of the US-trained Danab elite force in Jubaland, just a day after he publicly criticized the federal government, amid intensifying dispute with Jubaland’s leadership that threaten to ignite an all-out conflict.
Ahmed vehemently condemned authorities in Mogadishu for promoting military officers who had recently defected from Jubaland, asserting that Danab soldiers, who had long fought insurgents and made significant sacrifices, were unjustly overlooked, with their contributions dismissed and squandered.
Not only did Ahmed criticize the promotion of defected officers, but he also raised alarm over the large-scale deployment of government troops to Raskamboni, some 250 kilometers south of Kismayo, warning that the troop buildup, aimed at ousting the Jubaland leader, would only provide an opportunity for the militant group Al-Shabaab to exploit the escalating tensions.
Somali Army Chief Odowa Yusuf Rage, appointed by authorities just weeks ago to lead the offensive against the Jubaland administration, swiftly replaced Ahmed by appointing a subordinate officer to the vacated position.
Ahmed is not the sole commander to lose his position amid the intensifying standoff between Jubaland and the federal government; many other Jubaland military leaders have also been relieved of their duties and placed under house arrest, facing allegations of conspiring with federal authorities to orchestrate a covert coup against Jubaland leader Ahmed Madobe.
Contact us: info@somaliguardian.com

a2183.t:
By Seli Baisie
Afrobeats star King Promise has picked up two awards at the 26th Telecel Ghana Music Awards (TGMA), currently underway at the Grand Arena of the Accra International Conference Centre.
His hit single Paris won Best Afropop Song of the Year, a category packed with fierce competition. The song, which has enjoyed massive airplay and struck a chord with fans across the country, was recognised for its infectious blend of rhythm and lyrical appeal, solidifying King Promise’s place as one of Ghana’s most versatile music exports.
Moments after accepting the award, the Terminator hitmaker returned to the stage to collect his second win of the night, Afrobeats/Afropop Artiste of the Year, thanks in part to the success of his track Favourite Story.
The double win further cements King Promise’s dominance in the Afrobeats space and comes as he vies for the night’s most coveted title: Artiste of the Year.
In a brief speech, King Promise expressed gratitude to his fans and hinted that “he will be back,” suggesting more wins could be on the horizon.
The 26th edition of the TGMAs celebrates outstanding musical achievements in Ghana over the past year, bringing together industry heavyweights, rising stars, and fans for a night of recognition and live performances.

a2258.t:
- Researchers are linking rising temperatures to negative impacts on maternal, foetal and infant health.
- Data also links heat to preeclampsia, pre-term births, and complications in labour and childbirth.
- There is scope for the public health sector to become more active in climate action.
- Get the biggest business stories emailed to you every weekday, or go to the Fin24 front page.
Researchers around the world are drawing an ever-moredistinct line between rising global temperatures and negative effects onmaternal, foetal, and infant health. One of these researchers is ProfessorMatthew Chersich of the Wits RHI (Rural Health Institute), whose recent workhas focused on using data science to understand the effects of heat on pregnantmothers and their babies in Africa.
Chersich's first warning is that there is a double burden onAfrica as the continent is already being hit hardest by climate change but alsohas fewer resources to mount a sophisticated, wide-reaching, and sustainedresponse.
"The continent is already warming faster than otherregions in the world but is also a low carbon emitter," he said.
According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change,the northern and southern regions of the continent will become hotter and drierwhile the Sahel region will have increased rainfall.
"Right now we are in a phase of climate choice - the 10years we have left to do something and stop making nature our slave or thatchoice will cascade so that we won't have a choice because nature will be atits tipping point," he said. Chersich was speaking to Spotlight afterdelivering his inaugural lecture at Wits University at the end of August.
'How a medic came to study climate change'
In the lecture, titled "how a medic came to studyclimate change" Chersich recounted how seven years ago he and his familywere living in a small hamlet in Italy among a subsistence farming community.Increased extreme weather events quickly turned to lived reality and livedanxiety for the community that largely lived off the land. He experienced howhumans' continued ability to thrive on a planet pushed into decline wasslipping towards a precarious edge.
"Climate change and public health already intersect insome key areas, which makes this field an important new area of research thatwe in public health must be turning our attention to.
"Some of the intersections with the public healthresponse include how droughts and floods cause poverty and social disruption;there is also the response of emergency medicine in the case of increasedextreme weather events that destroy infrastructure; then there's work lookingat the effects on how climate change is shifting infectious disease patterns.All pathogens are temperature sensitive which means we'll see malaria spread tohigher altitude areas; and then there's work on maternal health, which is anarea where Wits University and I personally have a lot of background, so thisbecame an obvious area that I wanted to focus on."
Building on previous work
He said choosing to focus on maternal health was strategicbecause maternal health has been the starting point for many past public healthinterventions including a massive reduction in mother-to-child transmission ofHIV as well as interventions on nutrition and combating malaria.
Added to this, Chersich said, there was establishedfoundational work done by Wits researchers in the late 1990s that measured thematernal-foetal temperature gradient. "The research found that a foetus isabout half a degree warmer than its mother, which might not sound like much ofa difference but if the mother's temperature rises with a fever to 40 degrees,the foetus is at 40.5 degrees and that makes an enormous difference physiologically,"he said.
Impact of heat
Data from his research colleagues in Kenya is now showingthat heat can be linked to preeclampsia, pre-term births, and complications inlabour and childbirth - all of which can have knock-on effects for the motherand the child later on in life, he said.
Community health workers and women interviewed for Chersichand his colleagues' research have given revealing responses. These included: "Thefoetus is not at peace when it is hot; it only finds peace when it is born"or "it is difficult to push in the heat" and "the baby has comebefore its time because it is too hot".
"What is happening physiologically to cause thesepre-term impacts related to heat are changes to the endocrine system; oxidativeor inflammatory changes; changes in placental perfusion, which can change thecirculation of blood flow to the foetus that regulates heat; and there isincreased exposure and risk to infections that include food, water, andvector-borne infections," he said.
Chersich said the evidence points to a looming crisis formaternal health and infant health and means "public health must be morethan about treating disease".
Chersich set out a multi-layered intervention strategy. Acritical layer is using data science more effectively. One of the projectsChersich is now involved in is a five-year study that will span research teamsacross Africa and the United States.
"It involves individual participant data and will bethe largest data science project of its kind. Analysing this data will help usunlock some of the key questions and shape our interventions," he said.
More deliberate engagement
Chersich also said there is a need for the public healthsector to wake up to the necessity to enter more directly and deliberately intothe climate change space. One initiative he helped establish is
CHANCE (The Climate-Health Africa Network for Collaborationand Engagement), which is an initiative to bolster research that aligns thesetwo disciplines.
"The health sector is ripe to intervene and this shouldinclude making submissions for funding from the Green Climate Fund to do theresearch and put in place the kinds of strategies that will help those who willbe worst affected on the continent," he said.
"We in this sector understand the tricks and thetricksters. We know the playbook of big pharma, of the tobacco industry, thefood manufacturing industry, the meat industry, and now also the fossil fuelindustries," he said of the public health sector.
It's a terrible insight but he argues that it could holdstrategic advantage. It's a position from which to firm up boundaries withfunders and call for more accountability and transparency where there isconflict of interest. This while still compelling funders and donors - who maybe industrial polluters - to fund research and support interventions to curbfossil fuel dependence and reduce emissions.
Public health, he said, also understands how to manage bigglobal donors, citing long-standing PEPFAR and Global Fund projects on thecontinent. And public health initiatives are where a groundswell for policychange can also take root, Chersich said.
But even before policy, he said interventions need to startwith awareness on the ground. It could be healthcare workers knowing to makecool water available for pregnant women, especially during labour andchildbirth; better advice on planning pregnancy according to seasonaltemperatures; building more heat tolerant clinics and homes and planting moretrees. It is all underpinned by a fight still for poverty reduction andbuilding more equitable societies, he said.
Personal moral choice
Finally, Chersich used his inaugural lecture to bring homethe most uncomfortable message of them all and that is the link between climatechange and personal moral choice. Behavioural change, he said, will come withpersonal discomfort and personal sacrifice. It's eating less meat, taking fewerflights, consuming more mindfully and accumulating less.
For researchers and universities, he said, it is aboutquestioning relationships with funders and companies and industries thatadvance the fossil fuel dependency agenda and pay not to fix problems but for ablind eye turned, green-washing, and silence.
"We have an abusive relationship with nature. Itunderlies our problems. We think we can eat and eat [from] nature and it willjust replenish itself but there is no slowdown in emissions and we are on atrajectory of many places in the world being unliveable.
"All this means if we in public health want to fightdisease then we need to also [be] part of systemic change. We need to stop theeating," he said.
*This article was published by Spotlight - health journalismin the public interest.

a2274.t:
La Nation Bénin...
L’épi
d’arrêt de sable au port de Cotonou doit être réparé de façon définitive. Le
gouvernement s’inscrit dans cette dynamique et a décidé, lors du Conseil des
ministres du mercredi 11 septembre, de commanditer une étude à cette fin.
Alors
qu’il était réalisé en 2011 pour tenir pendant un demi-siècle, l’épi d’arrêt de
sable au port de Cotonou présente déjà des failles: des dégradations avancées qui
s’aggravent au fil des années. Ce qui nécessite une intervention urgente pour
que cette infrastructure financée par le Millennium challenge account (Mca)
puisse continuer à jouer son rôle dans la protection de la côte. C’est
conscient de cette réalité que le gouvernement a décidé de commanditer une
mission d’étude pour la réparation définitive de cet épi. 
Avant
cette initiative du gouvernement, la dégradation de l’infrastructure avait été
une source de discorde entre le port de Cotonou et le groupement l’ayant
réalisée. Les deux parties avaient alors, de manière consensuelle, choisi un
expert international indépendant. Il ressort du rapport de ce dernier que la
première cause de la défectuosité de l’infrastructure est la négligence dans sa
conception. Ce qui a conduit le groupement à effectuer une réparation
provisoire. Mais c’était peine perdue. La dégradation se poursuit encore, d’où
la décision du gouvernement d’opter pour une réparation définitive. 
Le
prolongement de l’épi d’arrêt de sable au port de Cotonou est une composante du
projet Accès aux Marchés du Programme Mca-Bénin. La construction de cette
infrastructure devrait permettre au sable qui s’entassait à l’entrée du bassin
portuaire et dans le chenal d’accès de s’accumuler à l’ouest de l’épi. Elle
devrait également permettre aux navires de grands tonnages d’accoster au port
de Cotonou, conformément aux ambitions du gouvernement.
Ces travaux qui se feront ne sont pas les seuls prévus pour la modernisation du port de Cotonou. Plusieurs autres chantiers sont ouverts à cet effet. Certains sont même déjà achevés et permettent à ce poumon de l’économie nationale d’accroître ses capacités.
Rénover les infrastructures obsolètes et augmenter la capacité du bassin portuaire pour accueillir des navires plus grands, tout en améliorant la qualité du service pour attirer du trafic supplémentaire, telle est l’ambition affichée à travers le Plan directeur du Port autonome de Cotonou (Pdp 2021-2026). Le programme d’investissement de cinq ans concocté à cet effet se compose de douze projets visant globalement à augmenter la capacité du port à plus de 20 millions de tonnes ainsi que l’efficacité de la manutention, tout en réduisant les temps d’attente pour les navires et les temps de transit pour les camions. Il s’agit aussi de développer le secteur de l’industrie portuaire du Bénin et de maintenir la position du port de Cotonou en tant que port de transit clé pour les pays enclavés tels que le Niger, Burkina Faso et Mali.
Le
financement total de ces projets s’élève à 461,6 millions d’euros, soit 302,8
milliards F Cfa. Ils seront financés par divers prêteurs ainsi que par les
capitaux propres du Port autonome de Cotonou (Pac), d’après la Note de synthèse
de Projet publiée par la Banque africaine de développement (Bad, juin 2023).
Pour
sa part, la Bad se positionne pour financer deux projets du Pdp: l’un concerne
la construction en cours du nouveau terminal vraquier (T5) à l’est du port avec
une capacité supplémentaire de 20 ha, qui sera dédié aux produits en vrac et
divers et l’autre, l’accès centralisé des camions en un seul point équipé de
barrières automatisées. Ce dernier projet vise la construction d’un parking
poids lourds sur un site de 13 ha à Zongo avec un système de gestion intégré et
digitalisé relié aux bases de données du port et du Guichet unique de commerce
extérieur (Guce) pour accélérer le traitement des marchandises. 
Géré
depuis 2018 par le Port d’Anvers-Bruges International (Pai), le port de Cotonou
est un port de transit qui assure 49 % d’import-export pour le Bénin (il
dessert 90 % du commerce international du pays) et 49 % de trafic de transit
dirigé vers le Niger (37 %), le Burkina Faso (4 %), le Mali (3 %) et le Nigeria
(5 %) et seulement 2 % de transbordement. Il dessert ainsi près de 100 millions
de consommateurs. En 2022, le port a traité près de 12 millions de tonnes de
marchandises, et le trafic devrait atteindre 23 millions de tonnes d’ici 2038.
A
l’horizon 2026, le Pac entend améliorer l’accès nautique et accroître la
compétitivité du fleuron de l’économie nationale.
L’image du port de Cotonou sortira davantage soignée à l'issue des travaux de construction du Centre des affaires maritimes. Tant la plateforme portuaire va améliorer son efficacité et l’épanouissement des acteurs qui y travaillent.
Le
Centre des affaires maritimes, c’est un cadre unique prévu pour accueillir tous
les acteurs portuaires des structures publiques et des entreprises privées
notamment les transitaires et commissionnaires en douane, les consignataires,
les services de douane, les importateurs, les transporteurs et autres. 
Une
fois construit, le centre permettra de désengorger le port et d’améliorer la
productivité. Situé à proximité du port, sur l’axe stratégique du Boulevard de
la Marina, le projet du Centre des affaires maritimes ambitionne de proposer
une solution fonctionnelle dans une optique d’impulser une nouvelle dynamique
aux structures publiques et privées travaillant en étroite collaboration avec
le Port autonome de Cotonou. La fluidité des opérations portuaires devenant
effective, cela va accroître la célérité dans l’enlèvement des marchandises et
l’augmentation des capacités opérationnelles au niveau des terminaux. 
Privilégiant
le travail collaboratif, il sera un lieu d’échanges et de créativité pour des
entreprises performantes.
Selon les prévisions, le Centre des affaires maritimes sera construit sur le site de l’ancien ministère des Infrastructures et des Transports qui était dans un état de vétusté très avancée. Déjà, le Conseil des ministres du 11 novembre 2020, a marqué son accord pour la contractualisation avec le bureau d’architectes Koffi & Diabaté pour la mission de maîtrise d’œuvre du projet. Ce choix est induit par la nécessité de recourir à des prestataires de grande expérience pour la conduite des études et la supervision des travaux au regard de la spécificité d’une telle infrastructure et des exigences liées à sa réalisation.
La
construction du centre fait partie des douze grands projets pour la
modernisation et l’attractivité du port de Cotonou
a2274.en:
La Nation Bénin...

Sand stoppage at the port of Cotonou: A study for a definitive repair of the groyne

The sand-arresting groyne at the port of Cotonou must be repaired definitively. The government is committed to this and decided, at the Council of Ministers of Wednesday 11 September, to commission a study to that end.

Although it was built in 2011 to last half a century, the sand-arresting groyne at the port of Cotonou already shows flaws: advanced deterioration that worsens over the years. This requires urgent intervention so that this infrastructure, financed by the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA), can continue to play its role in protecting the coast. Aware of this reality, the government decided to commission a study mission for the definitive repair of this groyne.

Before this government initiative, the deterioration of the infrastructure had been a source of discord between the port of Cotonou and the consortium that built it. The two parties then jointly chose an independent international expert. It emerges from his report that the primary cause of the infrastructure's defectiveness is negligence in its design. This led the consortium to carry out a provisional repair. But it was a wasted effort. The deterioration is still continuing, hence the government's decision to opt for a definitive repair.

The extension of the sand-arresting groyne at the port of Cotonou is a component of the Access to Markets project of the MCA-Benin Programme. The construction of this infrastructure was meant to allow the sand that piled up at the entrance of the port basin and in the access channel to accumulate to the west of the groyne. It was also meant to allow large-tonnage vessels to dock at the port of Cotonou, in line with the government's ambitions.

These works are not the only ones planned for the modernisation of the port of Cotonou. Several other projects are under way. Some are even already completed and are enabling this lung of the national economy to increase its capacity.

Renovating obsolete infrastructure and increasing the capacity of the port basin to accommodate larger vessels, while improving the quality of service to attract additional traffic: such is the ambition displayed through the Master Plan of the Autonomous Port of Cotonou (PDP 2021-2026). The five-year investment programme devised for this purpose consists of twelve projects aimed overall at increasing the port's capacity to more than 20 million tonnes as well as handling efficiency, while reducing waiting times for ships and transit times for trucks. It is also about developing Benin's port industry sector and maintaining the position of the port of Cotonou as a key transit port for landlocked countries such as Niger, Burkina Faso and Mali.

The total financing of these projects amounts to 461.6 million euros, or 302.8 billion CFA francs. They will be financed by various lenders as well as by the equity of the Autonomous Port of Cotonou (PAC), according to the Project Summary Note published by the African Development Bank (AfDB, June 2023).

For its part, the AfDB is positioning itself to finance two PDP projects: one concerns the ongoing construction of the new bulk terminal (T5) to the east of the port with an additional capacity of 20 hectares, which will be dedicated to bulk and miscellaneous products, and the other, the centralised access of trucks at a single point equipped with automated barriers. This latter project aims at the construction of a heavy-goods vehicle car park on a 13-hectare site at Zongo with an integrated and digitalised management system linked to the databases of the port and of the Single Window for Foreign Trade (GUCE) to speed up the processing of goods.

Managed since 2018 by Port of Antwerp-Bruges International (PAI), the port of Cotonou is a transit port that handles 49% of import-export for Benin (it serves 90% of the country's international trade) and 49% of transit traffic directed towards Niger (37%), Burkina Faso (4%), Mali (3%) and Nigeria (5%), and only 2% transhipment. It thus serves nearly 100 million consumers. In 2022, the port handled nearly 12 million tonnes of goods, and traffic is expected to reach 23 million tonnes by 2038.

By 2026, the PAC intends to improve nautical access and increase the competitiveness of the flagship of the national economy.

The image of the port of Cotonou will emerge further polished at the end of the construction works of the Maritime Business Centre. The port platform will improve its efficiency and the fulfilment of the actors who work there.

The Maritime Business Centre is a unique setting designed to host all port actors from public structures and private companies, notably freight forwarders and customs brokers, shipping agents, customs services, importers, transporters and others.

Once built, the centre will make it possible to decongest the port and improve productivity. Located close to the port, on the strategic axis of the Boulevard de la Marina, the Maritime Business Centre project aims to offer a functional solution with a view to giving new momentum to public and private structures working in close collaboration with the Autonomous Port of Cotonou. As the fluidity of port operations becomes effective, this will increase the speed of goods removal and the expansion of operational capacity at the terminals.

Favouring collaborative work, it will be a place of exchange and creativity for high-performing companies.

According to forecasts, the Maritime Business Centre will be built on the site of the former Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport, which was in a very advanced state of dilapidation. Already, the Council of Ministers of 11 November 2020 gave its agreement for contracting with the architectural firm Koffi & Diabaté for the project management mission of the project. This choice was prompted by the need to use highly experienced providers for conducting the studies and supervising the works, given the specificity of such infrastructure and the requirements linked to its execution.

The construction of the centre is one of the twelve major projects for the modernisation and attractiveness of the port of Cotonou.

a2344.t:
La Nation Bénin...
Septembre
1999 - Septembre 2024. Care International fête ses 25 ans d’engagement au
service des communautés vulnérables au Bénin. Les manifestations marquant cet
anniversaire ont été lancées, ce lundi 2 septembre à Cotonou, à la faveur d’un
webinaire qui retrace les prouesses mais aussi les défis de l’organisation.
Succès,
fierté et engagement au profit des communautés vulnérables et marginalisées…
Care International, une organisation humanitaire de renommée mondiale, célèbre
cette année un quart de siècle de présence et d’impact au Bénin. L'organisation
a initié dans ce cadre une série d'événements visant à mettre en lumière son
parcours, ses réalisations et ses ambitions pour les années à venir, dont un
webinaire organisé ce lundi 2 septembre à Cotonou.
Depuis
la signature de l’accord de siège intervenue le 9 septembre 1999 au Bénin, Care
a joué un rôle crucial dans l’amélioration des conditions de vie des
communautés et le renforcement des capacités des partenaires locaux, laisse
entendre Guillaume Aguettant, directeur pays Care Bénin/Togo, qui a lancé les
premières activités de l’Ong au niveau local. En vingt-cinq années d’existence,
se réjouit-il, Care Bénin s’est imposée comme un acteur clé du développement,
opérant dans les 77 communes du pays avec une forte concentration dans les
quatre départements du Nord. A preuve, en 2023, l’organisation a pu toucher
près de 500 000 personnes à travers 21 projets de développement et deux projets
humanitaires, avec un budget total de 14,37 millions de dollars soit 8,69
milliards F Cfa, indique M. Aguettant.
Les
témoignages des participants aux programmes et projets (politiques, élèves,
anciens détenus et autres anonymes), de partenaires de mise en œuvre
(responsables d’Ong locales) et d’anciens membres du staff de l’organisation
recueillis à travers un film documentaire et lors du webinaire sont élogieux.
Care Bénin a contribué à « changer la vie » de plus d’un, à travers la lutte
contre les violences basées sur le genre, l’accroissement du leadership des
jeunes filles et des femmes, la prévention des conflits et la préparation aux
catastrophes, la gouvernance et la redevabilité sociale, l’alimentation et la nutrition
et la santé sexuelle et de la reproduction.
L’organisation se distingue par son personnel dynamique et engagé, avec une forte représentation de jeunes de moins de 35 ans et constitue une famille d’éclosion et d’épanouissements des talents au service des communautés, salue Claudine Awuté Mensah, vice-présidente chargée des Programmes et Opérations Care International, ancienne directrice pays de Care Bénin/Togo. Elle est appuyée par Balla Sidibé, directeur régional de Care pour l'Afrique de l’Ouest, qui souligne que Care a su bâtir un réseau de partenaires solide et diversifié, incluant des institutions internationales comme l’Usaid, la Banque mondiale, l’Union européenne, le Royaume des Pays-Bas, la Coopération Suisse ainsi que des membres de Care International tels que Care Usa, Care France, Care Luxembourg, Care Canada, pour ne citer que ceux-là. Cette diversité de partenariats permet à l’organisation de conduire des projets multisectoriels répondant aux besoins des populations les plus vulnérables, indique-t-il.
Care Bénin réaffirme son engagement à poursuivre son travail dans quatre domaines prioritaires : la justice économique et le genre, la santé de la mère, de l’enfant et du jeune, la sécurité alimentaire et nutritionnelle, ainsi que la préparation et la réponse aux urgences, assure Alain Troukou, directeur de la Qualité des programmes et de la Mobilisation des ressources. Avec l’ambition de toucher 2,8 millions de personnes d’ici 2026, l’organisation se projette dans l’avenir avec la volonté de contribuer à vaincre la pauvreté et l’injustice sociale, poursuit-il.
Dans
le cadre des festivités, une journée portes ouvertes aura lieu lundi 9
septembre prochain, et sera marquée par une séance de don de sang. Suivra du 18
au 20 septembre la participation à la Gaani de la Gnon Kogui aux côtés de la
vice-présidente de la République. Care Bénin a également prévu un café-débat,
le 28 septembre prochain, pour marquer la Journée mondiale du droit à
l'interruption volontaire de grossesse (Ivg)■
a2344.en:
Sustainable development: Care Bénin celebrates 25 years of impact and commitment

La Nation Bénin...

September 1999 – September 2024. Care International is celebrating 25 years of commitment in the service of vulnerable communities in Benin. The events marking this anniversary were launched this Monday 2 September in Cotonou with a webinar retracing the organisation's achievements and also its challenges.

Success, pride and commitment for the benefit of vulnerable and marginalised communities… Care International, a world-renowned humanitarian organisation, this year celebrates a quarter of a century of presence and impact in Benin. In this context, the organisation has launched a series of events to highlight its journey, its achievements and its ambitions for the years to come, including a webinar held on Monday 2 September in Cotonou.

Since the signing of the headquarters agreement on 9 September 1999 in Benin, Care has played a crucial role in improving the living conditions of communities and building the capacity of local partners, says Guillaume Aguettant, country director of Care Bénin/Togo, who launched the NGO's first activities at local level. In twenty-five years of existence, he says with satisfaction, Care Bénin has established itself as a key development actor, operating in all 77 communes of the country with a strong concentration in the four northern departments. As evidence, in 2023 the organisation was able to reach nearly 500,000 people through 21 development projects and two humanitarian projects, with a total budget of 14.37 million dollars, or 8.69 billion CFA francs, Mr Aguettant indicates.

The testimonies of participants in the programmes and projects (politicians, pupils, former detainees and other anonymous people), of implementing partners (heads of local NGOs) and of former members of the organisation's staff, gathered through a documentary film and during the webinar, are laudatory. Care Bénin has helped to "change the life" of many, through the fight against gender-based violence, the increased leadership of girls and women, conflict prevention and disaster preparedness, governance and social accountability, food and nutrition, and sexual and reproductive health.

The organisation stands out for its dynamic and committed staff, with a strong representation of young people under 35, and constitutes a family in which talents emerge and flourish in the service of communities, praises Claudine Awuté Mensah, vice-president for Programmes and Operations at Care International and former country director of Care Bénin/Togo. She is supported by Balla Sidibé, Care's regional director for West Africa, who stresses that Care has been able to build a solid and diversified network of partners, including international institutions such as USAID, the World Bank, the European Union, the Kingdom of the Netherlands and Swiss Cooperation, as well as members of Care International such as Care USA, Care France, Care Luxembourg and Care Canada, to name only those. This diversity of partnerships enables the organisation to run multisectoral projects responding to the needs of the most vulnerable populations, he indicates.

Care Bénin reaffirms its commitment to continuing its work in four priority areas: economic justice and gender, the health of mothers, children and young people, food and nutrition security, and emergency preparedness and response, assures Alain Troukou, director of Programme Quality and Resource Mobilisation. With the ambition of reaching 2.8 million people by 2026, the organisation looks to the future with the will to contribute to defeating poverty and social injustice, he continues.

As part of the festivities, an open day will be held next Monday 9 September, marked by a blood donation session. This will be followed from 18 to 20 September by participation in the Gaani of the Gnon Kogui alongside the Vice-President of the Republic. Care Bénin has also planned a café-debate on 28 September to mark the World Day for the Right to Abortion (IVG).

a2440.t:
The United States has announced an allocation of over $22 million in additional aid to boost resilience and food security for the most vulnerable populations in Madagascar.
The funding, through the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), marks the initiation of two new five-year projects aimed at enhancing resilience and food security in the Androy, Anosy and Atsimo Atsinanana regions of Madagascar.
The assistance is designed to benefit about 88,000 households that are identified as extremely impoverished and marginalised.
“This assistance, which will be implemented by consortiums led by USAID partners Catholic Relief Services and Cultivating New Frontiers in Agriculture, will support marginalized households to build sustainable livelihoods, develop financial capital and increase their savings and assets,” USAID said in a statement.
It will also support households to access existing health, nutrition, and water, sanitation, and hygiene services, and bolster households’ capacity to withstand future shocks and stresses.
The initiative complements USAID’s ongoing emergency programmes in response to cyclical crises such as droughts and cyclones in Madagascar.
In 2024 alone, the United States has already contributed nearly $103 million towards humanitarian aid efforts in Madagascar.
JN/APA

a2482.t:
KATIMA MULILO – Ndumeleti wa naha ya United States (US) Brandon Hudspeth unyatezi tuso yanaha US kwa naha Namibia kakatengo ka PEPFAR. Hudspeth, azamaya ni Taimi Amaambo, mubakweli muetapili wa likolo la Makete ni Pabalelo ya Sicaba, viki yefelile nebaile kuyo tatuba miyaho ye tusiwa ki PEPFAR, kungelela cwalo ni sipatelanyana sa Katima Mulilo hamoho cwalo ni malabalatoli ni sipatelanyana sa Walvis Bay Corridor.
Poto ki kalulo ya kutabela lilimo zemashumi amabeli za PEPFAR zakufumaneha mwanaha Namibia, kusupeza likezo za tiululo hala kakokwani ka HIV ni TB. Mubusisi wa sikiliti sa Zambezi Dorothy Kabula nalumbile naha US katuso yetuna.
“Ki taba yende. Lusweli kueza hande hala makete aluna mwanaha Namibia. Naha US ibile mwasilikani ni Namibia nako yetelele. Lusweli kueza hande kwaneku la makete mwanaha Namibia. Muzwelepili kueza cwalo. Musike mwafelisa milyani yeo. Silikani si swanela kuzwelapili ni naha Namibia,” nabulezi.
Hudspeth nahatelezi hala moya wa swalisano hala zende ze ezizwe mwanaha Namibia. “Nibata kuhatelela fataba ya swalisano kakuli, ee, naha US ifile tuso ni likelezo, kono ki swalisano ni banaha Namibia, likolo la makete, kokutisize kuli likezo ze lieze hande. Lubile ni lisebelezo za PEPFAR mwalinaha zeñwi, kono hali bonahali moli bonahalela mwanaha Namibia… kikabaka la mina,” nabulezi.
Ha nyatisisa fa poto naekelize kuli, “Ibile poto yende, sihulu kaswalisano ni likolo la makete. Taba yene tabisa hahulu ki kuikopanya ni bakuli nikulemuha kamuhelo yabona hala taba ye ni tuso ya kuitambeka kwamasika asa taha. Kona mutomo walika kaufela,” nabulezi. Amaambo nabulezi hala butokwa bwa swalisano mwamilelo mwahala Namibia ni mubuso wanaha US.
“Sesitisa ku ketahana mwahala swalisano ye kikuli milelo yaluna kaufela, ki ya swalisano, kuongaonga likezo hamoho. Hakikuli mubuso wanaha US ubulela kuli ‘ze kona ze muswanela ku eza.’ Kono, ki litokwahalo zelu lemuha hamoho. Ki kabaka leo lukona kubona batu base bali baelezi, ba ba pila ni kakokwani ka HIV, ni kutusa babañwi babali mwa mayemo aswana,” nabulezi.
Na ekelize kuli swalisano yeo ki ye fita miyaho ya makete. Poto hape ne ndongwama mitomo ye mine: kutabela lilimo zemashumi amabeli mwanaha Namibia, kutalima zwelopili ya bukamuso sakata, kusupeza butungi bwa silikani sa US ni Namibia, ni ponahazo ya buitumelo kwa babeleki ba makete. Linaha zepeli lizwelapili kuitama ku alabela kwa matuku a TB ni HIV, ili kuli kuno kutahiswa cinceho kwa sicaba sa naha Namibia, sihulu mwa libaka zamatakanyani sina mwasikiliti sa Zambezi.
a2482.en:
US, Namibia praise cooperation in health

KATIMA MULILO - The United States (US) representative (Charge d'Affaires) Brandon Hudspeth has highlighted US support to Namibia through PEPFAR. Hudspeth, travelling with Taimi Amaambo, Deputy Executive Director of the Ministry of Health and Social Services, last week visited facilities supported by PEPFAR, including the Katima Mulilo clinic as well as laboratories and the Walvis Bay Corridor clinic.

The visit is part of celebrating 20 years of PEPFAR in Namibia, showcasing the work done to fight HIV and TB. The Governor of the Zambezi Region, Dorothy Kabula, praised the US for its great support.

"It is a good thing. We are doing well in our health services in Namibia. The US has been a friend of Namibia for a long time. We are doing well on the health side in Namibia. Keep on doing so. Do not stop those medicines. The friendship with Namibia should continue," she said.

Hudspeth emphasised the spirit of partnership behind the successes achieved in Namibia. "I want to emphasise the issue of partnership because, yes, the US has provided support and technical advice, but it is the partnership with Namibians, with the health ministry, that has made these programmes succeed. We have had PEPFAR services in other countries, but they do not look the way they look in Namibia... it is because of you," he said.

Reflecting on the visit he added, "It has been a good visit, especially because of the partnership with the health ministry. What was most encouraging was meeting patients and seeing how they have embraced this and the benefit of passing it on to coming generations. That is the foundation of everything," he said. Amaambo spoke about the importance of partnership in planning between Namibia and the US government.

"What makes this partnership distinctive is that all our plans are joint, we organise activities together. It is not that the US government says 'this is what you must do.' Rather, they are needs that we identify together. That is why we can see people who are now counsellors, who live with HIV, helping others who are in the same situation," she said.

She added that the partnership goes beyond health facilities. The visit also had four objectives: celebrating 20 years in Namibia, looking at prospects for a sustainable future, showcasing the depth of the friendship between the US and Namibia, and expressing gratitude to health workers. The two countries continue to commit to responding to TB and HIV, so as to bring change to the people of Namibia, especially in rural areas such as the Zambezi Region.

a2552.t:
Rural areas damaged by conflicts, with estimated inhabitants of eight million people, foresee humanitarian assistance from the European Union (EU). The EU will donate 35 million euros to support the Productive Safety Net Program (PSNP), now beginning its fifth phase to provide food, job, health, and social caregiving sectors and services. The overall budget for the five-year program will be 2.38 billion dollars. Solomon Kebede, press and information officer, said the EU has been working with the program since its launch in 2005. It was introduced after the most hotly contested national elections that year when donors felt their trust was breached following widespread clampdown. A series of protests in Addis Abeba and other towns against what the opposition claimed were rigged elections outcomes led to the death of hundreds of people. Donors, mainly from the EU, discontinued providing direct budget support, replacing it with PNSP. Roland Kobia, EU's ambassador, and the World Bank Country Directors, agriculture and finance ministries' representatives are expected to attend the ceremony on Monday, December 12, 2022, at the EU office on Cape Verde St. In 2011, a severe drought in 60 years affected the Eastern Africa region, causing famine in Somalia and acute hunger and malnutrition in northern Kenya. Ethiopia managed the crisis without experiencing famine. During the 2015-16 El Nino droughts, which resulted in millions of Ethiopians requiring emergency food assistance, PSNP was hailed for demonstrating how contingency arrangements could be used during emergencies.
[ssba-buttons]

a2701.t:
Les pays de l'Alliance du Sahel comptent sur l'aide de la Russie pour créer une industrie militaire
Les pays de l'Alliance du Sahel comptent sur l'aide de la Russie pour créer une industrie militaire
C'est ce qu'a déclaré à Sputnik le ministre malien des Affaires étrangères Abdoulaye Diop .
"Nous travaillons déjà avec la Russie sur plusieurs projets, que ce soit dans le domaine sécuritaire comme dans le domaine de la diplomatie ou sur le plan économique, nos pays souhaitent renforcer nos capacités, développer une autonomie, pour que nous sortions des schémas de dépendance", a-t-il déclaré.
L’acquisition d’équipements militaires devient un besoin de plus en plus important, a souligné le ministre.
Les pays de l'AES essayeront "de faire en sorte qu'avec le partenaire russe qui a une technologie, une expérience avérée, que, en conjonction avec les entreprises et l'État russe, que nous puissions aussi créer des capacités militaires dans l'espace AES", a-t-il ajouté.
Cela réduira leur "dépendance par rapport aux importations d'équipements militaires" et créera de nouveaux emplois.
Les chefs des diplomaties du Mali, du Burkina Faso et du Niger se sont rendus à Moscou début avril à l'invitation de leur homologue russe Sergueï Lavrov dans le cadre des premières consultations entre l'Alliance des États du Sahel et la Russie.
a2701.en:
The countries of the Sahel Alliance are counting on Russia's help to create a military industry

The countries of the Sahel Alliance are counting on Russia's help to create a military industry.

This was stated to Sputnik by Mali's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Abdoulaye Diop.

"We are already working with Russia on several projects, whether in the security field, in the field of diplomacy or on the economic level; our countries wish to strengthen our capacities and develop autonomy, so that we can move out of patterns of dependence," he said.

The acquisition of military equipment is becoming an increasingly important need, the minister stressed.

The AES countries will try "to ensure that, with the Russian partner, which has technology and proven experience, in conjunction with Russian companies and the Russian state, we can also create military capacities within the AES area," he added.

This will reduce their "dependence on imports of military equipment" and will create new jobs.

The heads of diplomacy of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger travelled to Moscow in early April at the invitation of their Russian counterpart Sergei Lavrov, as part of the first consultations between the Alliance of Sahel States and Russia.
